dictNote: The Avvim, also spelled Avims, were a pre-Israelite people who lived in villages in the region of Gaza before being driven out and largely destroyed by the Caphtorim, migrants from Crete associated with the Philistines (Deuteronomy 2:23; Joshua 13:3). The same Hebrew name is applied in 2 Kings 17:31 to settlers from Avva whom the Assyrians relocated to Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom's population; those settlers brought their own gods, Nibhaz and Tartak, with them.

name: Habor
dictNote: The united stream, or, according to others, with beautiful banks, the name of a river in Assyria, and also of the district through which it flowed (1 Chr. 5:26). There is a river called Khabur which rises in the central highlands of Kurdistan, and flows south-west till it falls into the Tigris, about 70 miles above Mosul. This was not, however, the Habor of Scripture. There is another river of the same name (the Chaboras) which, after a course of about 200 miles, flows into the Euphrates at Karkesia, the ancient Circesium. This was, there can be little doubt, the ancient Habor.

name: Gatam
dictNote: Gatam was a son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau who became one of the clan chiefs, or “dukes,” of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 16; 1 Chronicles 1:36). Like his brothers, he is remembered only as the eponymous head of an Edomite clan in the genealogical lists.

name: Gennesaret
note: Gennesaret (i.e. Kinnereth), a lake and plain in Palestine
dictNote: Gennesaret refers both to a fertile plain on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee and, by extension, to the lake itself, also called the Sea of Galilee or Chinnereth in the Old Testament (Matthew 14:34; Mark 6:53; Luke 5:1). The first-century historian Josephus praised the plain's exceptional fertility, describing it as supporting nearly every kind of tree and crop through most of the year. A first-century fishing boat recovered from the mud near Kibbutz Ginosar on the lakeshore in 1986 has illustrated the fishing economy the Gospels describe in this same area.

name: Shunem

secondTemple.excerpt: 1096.] About the same time, the Philistines resolved to make war against the Israelites; and sent to all their confederates that they would go along with them to the war to Reggan, [near the city Shunem 20 ], whence they might gather themselves together, and suddenly attack the Hebrews.

dictNote: Two resting-places, a little village in the tribe of Issachar, to the north of Jezreel and south of Mount Gilboa (Josh. 19:18), where the Philistines encamped when they came against Saul (1 Sam. 28:4), and where Elisha was hospitably entertained by a rich woman of the place. On the sudden death of this woman’s son she hastened to Carmel, 20 miles distant across the plain, to tell Elisha, and to bring him with her to Shunem. There, in the “prophet’s chamber,” the dead child lay; and Elisha entering it, shut the door and prayed earnestly: and the boy was restored to life (2 Kings 4:8-37). This woman afterwards retired during the famine to the low land of the Philistines; and on returning a few years afterwards, found her house and fields in the possession of a stranger. She appealed to the king at Samaria, and had them in a somewhat remarkable manner restored to her (comp. 2 Kings 8:1-6).

name: Miletus
note: Miletus, a city of Asia Minor
dictNote: (Miletum, 2 Tim. 4:20), a seaport town and the ancient capital of Ionia, about 36 miles south of Ephesus. On his voyage from Greece to Syria, Paul touched at this port, and delivered that noble and pathetic address to the elders (“presbyters,” ver. 28) of Ephesus recorded in Acts 20:15-35. The site of Miletus is now some 10 miles from the coast. (See EPHESIANS, EPISTLE TO.)

name: Zephi
dictNote: Zephi, also spelled Zepho, was a son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau, listed among the clan chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11; 1 Chronicles 1:36). Nothing beyond his place in this genealogy is recorded of him.

name: Beer-lahai-roi
note: Beer-Lachai-Roi, a place in the Desert
dictNote: I.e., “the well of him that liveth and seeth me,” or, as some render it, “the well of the vision of life”, the well where the Lord met with Hagar (Gen. 16:7-14). Isaac dwelt beside this well (24:62; 25:11). It has been identified with ‘Ain Muweileh, or Moilahhi, south-west of Beersheba, and about 12 miles W. from Kadesh-barnea.

name: Azur
note: Azzur, the name of three Israelites
dictNote: Azur (properly Azzur, meaning “he that assists”) is the name of at least three men in the Old Testament: a covenant-signer under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:17), the father of the false prophet Hananiah who broke Jeremiah's symbolic yoke and predicted a swift return from exile that never came (Jeremiah 28:1), and the father of Jaazaniah, one of the corrupt princes Ezekiel saw plotting evil counsel in a vision (Ezekiel 11:1).

dictNote: Asenath was an Egyptian woman, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On (Heliopolis), whom Pharaoh gave to Joseph as his wife (Genesis 41:45). She bore Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, who became the ancestors of two of Israel's twelve tribes (Genesis 41:50-52; 46:20). Her marriage into an Egyptian priestly family reflects Joseph's full integration into Egyptian court life during his rise to power under Pharaoh.

name: Hegai
note: Hege or Hegai, a eunuch of Xerxes
dictNote: Hegai was the eunuch in charge of King Ahasuerus's harem at Susa who managed the young women, including Esther, brought in for the king's consideration (Esther 2:8). He took a particular liking to Esther and gave her preferential treatment, cosmetics, servants, and the best place in the harem, which likely improved her chances of being chosen queen (Esther 2:9, 15).

name: Pelaiah
note: Pelajah, the name of three Israelites
dictNote: Pelaiah's name means “the LORD has distinguished.” One man of this name appears in the royal genealogy as a descendant of David after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:24). A second Pelaiah was a Levite who helped explain the law to the people after Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:7) and later signed Nehemiah's covenant (Nehemiah 10:10).

dictNote: Trees, (Ex. 15:27; Num. 33:9), the name of the second station where the Israelites encamped after crossing the Red Sea. It had “twelve wells of water and threescore and ten palm trees.” It has been identified with the Wady Ghurundel, the most noted of the four wadies which descend from the range of et-Tih towards the sea. Here they probably remained some considerable time. The form of expression in Ex. 16:1 seems to imply that the people proceeded in detachments or companies from Elim, and only for the first time were assembled as a complete host when they reached the wilderness of Sin (q.v.).

name: Shimeah
dictNote: Shimeah was one of David's brothers, a son of Jesse, and the father of Jonadab, the shrewd nephew who advised Amnon in his plot against Tamar (2 Samuel 13:3); he is also called Shimea elsewhere. A second, unrelated Shimeah was a Benjamite descended from Gibeon, also known as Shimeam (1 Chronicles 8:32; 9:38).

name: Omega
note: the last letter of the Greek alphabet, i.e. (figuratively) the finality
dictNote: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, paired with Alpha, the first letter, in the divine self-description “I am Alpha and Omega,” found three times in Revelation (1:8; 21:6; 22:13). The phrase functions as a title, not a name, declaring God, and in 22:13 Christ, as the beginning and end of all things, encompassing everything in between. The imagery draws on a common ancient rhetorical device of using the first and last letters of an alphabet to signify totality.

name: Didymus
note: double, i.e. twin; Didymus, a Christian
dictNote: Didymus is the Greek word for “twin,” used in John's Gospel as a byname for the apostle Thomas (John 11:16; 20:24; 21:2). John likely includes the translation because some readers knew Thomas primarily by this descriptive nickname rather than his Aramaic name. No biblical tradition identifies who his twin sibling was.

name: Salma
note: Salma, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Salma, also spelled Salmon, was the son of Nahshon, a leader of the tribe of Judah, and the father of Boaz through his marriage to Rahab of Jericho, according to the genealogies in Ruth 4:20-21 and Matthew 1:5. Chronicles also remembers him as the ancestor, or founding patriarch, of Bethlehem and several related Judahite clans (1 Chronicles 2:11, 51, 54). Through Boaz and Ruth, his line runs directly to David and, in Matthew's genealogy, to Jesus.

dictNote: A watch-mountain or a watch-tower. In the heart of the mountains of Israel, a few miles north-west of Shechem, stands the “hill of Shomeron,” a solitary mountain, a great “mamelon.” It is an oblong hill, with steep but not inaccessible sides, and a long flat top. Omri, the king of Israel, purchased this hill from Shemer its owner for two talents of silver, and built on its broad summit the city to which he gave the name of “Shomeron”, i.e., Samaria, as the new capital of his kingdom instead of Tirzah (1 Kings 16:24). As such it possessed many advantages. Here Omri resided during the last six years of his reign. As the result of an unsuccessful war with Syria, he appears to have been obliged to grant to the Syrians the right to “make streets in Samaria”, i.e., probably permission to the Syrian merchants to carry on their trade in the Israelite capital. This would imply the existence of a considerable Syrian population. “It was the only great city of Palestine created by the sovereign. All the others had been already consecrated by patriarchal tradition or previous possession. But Samaria was the choice of Omri alone. He, indeed, gave to the city which he had built the name of its former owner, but its especial connection with himself as its founder is proved by the designation which it seems Samaria bears in Assyrian inscriptions, Beth-khumri (‘the house or palace of Omri’).”, Stanley. Samaria was frequently besieged. In the days of Ahab, Benhadad II. came up against it with thirty-two vassal kings, but was defeated with a great slaughter (1 Kings 20:1-21). A second time, next year, he assailed it; but was again utterly routed, and was compelled to surrender to Ahab (20:28-34), whose army, as compared with that of Benhadad, was no more than “two little flocks of kids.” In the days of Jehoram this Benhadad again laid siege to Samaria, during which the city was reduced to the direst extremities. But just when success seemed to be within their reach, they suddenly broke up the seige, alarmed by a mysterious noise of chariots and horses and a great army, and fled, leaving their camp with all its contents behind them. The famishing inhabitants of the city were soon relieved with the abundance of the spoil of the Syrian camp; and it came to pass, according to the word of Elisha, that “a measure of fine flour was sold for a shekel, and two measures of barely for a shekel, in the gates of Samaria” (2 Kings 7:1-20). Shalmaneser invaded Israel in the days of Hoshea, and reduced it to vassalage. He laid siege to Samaria (B.C. 723), which held out for three years, and was at length captured by Sargon, who completed the conquest Shalmaneser had begun (2 Kings 18:9-12; 17:3), and removed vast numbers of the tribes into captivity. (See SARGON.) This city, after passing through various vicissitudes, was given by the emperor Augustus to Herod the Great, who rebuilt it, and called it Sebaste (Gr. form of Augustus) in honour of the emperor. In the New Testament the only mention of it is in Acts 8:5-14, where it is recorded that Philip went down to the city of Samaria and preached there. It is now represented by the hamlet of Sebustieh, containing about three hundred inhabitants. The ruins of the ancient town are all scattered over the hill, down the sides of which they have rolled. The shafts of about one hundred of what must have been grand Corinthian columns are still standing, and attract much attention, although nothing definite is known regarding them. (Comp. Micah 1:6.) In the time of Christ, Western Palestine was divided into three provinces, Judea, Samaria, and Galilee. Samaria occupied the centre of Palestine (John 4:4). It is called in the Talmud the “land of the Cuthim,” and is not regarded as a part of the Holy Land at all. It may be noticed that the distance between Samaria and Jerusalem, the respective capitals of the two kingdoms, is only 35 miles in a direct line.

name: Uthai
note: Uthai, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Uthai's name means “helpful.” One Uthai was a descendant of Judah through Perez who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:4). A second man of the same name led a group of exiles back from Babylon with Ezra (Ezra 8:14).

name: Amittai
dictNote: Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah, identified as a native of Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25; Jonah 1:1). Nothing else is recorded of him beyond this identification.

name: Shelomith (from the margin)
note: Shelomoth, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Shelomith is a marginal spelling variant, the main text reads “Shelomoth,” attached to two Levites in Chronicles: a leader of a division of the Kohathite family descended from Izhar and Moses (1 Chronicles 24:22) and a Levite in charge of the temple treasuries under David (1 Chronicles 26:25-26). It is uncertain whether these references point to one man or two, since Chronicles' genealogical lists frequently repeat family names across generations.

name: Adoniram
dictNote: Adoniram, also called Adoram, was the son of Abda and served as the official in charge of forced labor levies under David, Solomon, and briefly Rehoboam (2 Samuel 20:24; 1 Kings 4:6; 1 Kings 12:18). When Rehoboam sent him to enforce the labor tax on the northern tribes after Solomon's death, the people stoned him to death, an act that helped trigger the kingdom's split into Israel and Judah (1 Kings 12:18).

name: Telem
note: Telem, the name of a place in Idumaea, also of a temple doorkeeper
dictNote: Oppression. (1.) A porter of the temple in the time of Ezra (10:24). (2.) A town in the southern border of Judah (Josh. 15:24); probably the same as Telaim.

name: Lebana
note: Lebana or Lebanah, one of the Nethinim
dictNote: Lebana, also spelled Lebanah, was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:45; Nehemiah 7:48). Nothing further is recorded of him.

name: Taberah
note: Taberah, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Burning, a place in the wilderness of Paran, where the “fire of the Lord” consumed the murmuring Israelites (Num. 11:3; Deut. 9:22). It was also called Kibroth-hattaavah (q.v.).

name: Mithredath
note: Mithredath, the name of two Persians
dictNote: Mithredath, a Hebrew form of the Persian name Mithridates meaning “given by Mithra,” was the royal treasurer of Cyrus who, at the king's command, returned the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had looted from Jerusalem to the returning exiles (Ezra 1:8). A different Mithredath was a Persian official in Samaria who joined other local officials in writing a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7).

name: Tahan
note: Tachan, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Tahan was a descendant of Ephraim and the ancestral head of the Tahanite clan (Numbers 26:35). In the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles 7:25, he appears as the son of Telah rather than directly of Ephraim, one of several small discrepancies between the tribal lists.

name: Eliahbah
dictNote: Eliahba was a Shaalbonite listed among David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:32; 1 Chronicles 11:33). No details of his deeds are recorded beyond his inclusion in this roll of honor.

name: Beth-Nimrah
note: Beth-Nimrah, a place east of the Jordan
dictNote: (house of leopards) one of the fenced cities on the east of Jordan taken and built by the tribe of Gad (Numbers 32:36) and described as being in the valley beside Beth-haran. (Joshua 13:27) In (Numbers 32:3) it is called simply Nimrah. The name still survives in the modern Nahr Nimrim, above Jericho on the Jordan.

name: Japhlet
dictNote: Japhlet was a descendant of Asher through Beriah and the head of a family clan within the tribe, the Japhletites (1 Chronicles 7:32-33). Nothing else is known of him.

name: Masrekah
dictNote: Vineyard of noble vines, a place in Idumea, the native place of Samlah, one of the Edomitish kings (Gen. 36:36; 1 Chr. 1:47).

name: Mecholathite
note: a Mecholathite or inhabitant of Abel-Mecholah

name: Avith
note: Avvith (or Avvoth), a place in Palestine

secondTemple.excerpt: And ’Asâm died, and ’Adâth,  the son of Barad,  who slew Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead, and the name of his city was Avith.

dictNote: (ruins), the city of Hadad ben-Bedad, one of the kings of Edom before there were kings in Israel. (Genesis 36:35; 1 Chronicles 1:46)

name: Ulai
note: the Ulai (or Eulaeus), a river of Persia
dictNote: The Eulaus of the Greeks; a river of Susiana. It was probably the eastern branch of the Choasper (Kerkhan), which divided into two branches some 20 miles above the city of Susa. Hence Daniel (8:2, 16) speaks of standing “between the banks of Ulai”, i.e., between the two streams of the divided river.

name: Azorigin
dictNote: Azor appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Eliakim and the father of Zadok, one link in the postexilic chain connecting Zerubbabel to Joseph, husband of Mary (Matthew 1:13-14). He is not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture and has no independent narrative beyond this genealogical placement.

name: Zilthai
note: Tsillethai, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Zilthai's name means “shadow of the LORD.” One Zilthai was a Benjamite family head (1 Chronicles 8:20). A second Zilthai was a captain from the tribe of Manasseh who defected to join David's forces at Ziklag while David was still fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:20).

name: Jedaiah
note: Jedajah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Jedaiah was a common priestly name in the postexilic period, borne by several priests who returned from Babylonian exile and served in the rebuilt temple.

name: Gallim

secondTemple.excerpt: 17 For as to Michal, the daughter of King Saul, who had been David’s wife, her father had given her in marriage to Phalti, the son of Laish, who was of the city of Gallim.

dictNote: Heaps, (1 Sam. 25:44; Isa. 10:30). The native place of Phalti, to whom Michal was given by Saul. It was probably in Benjamin, to the north of Jerusalem.

name: Jokmeam
dictNote: Gathering of the people, a city of Ephraim, which was given with its suburbs to the Levites (1 Chr. 6:68). It lay somewhere in the Jordan valley (1 Kings 4:12, R.V.; but in A.V. incorrectly “Jokneam”).

name: Hammon
note: Chammon, the name of two places in Palestine

secondTemple.excerpt:
As an instance of which, Alexander journeyed over a country without water, in the heat of summer, to the oracle of [Jupiter] Hammon, and quickly passed over the Bay of Pamphylia, when, by Divine Providence, the sea was cut off — thus Providence restraining the sea on his account, as it had sent him rain when he traveled [over the desert].\"
N.

dictNote: Hammon refers to two separate towns in the Old Testament: one in the territory of Asher near Sidon (Joshua 19:28), likely identified with modern Umm el-Amoud, and a Levitical city assigned to the tribe of Naphtali (1 Chronicles 6:76), probably the same place as Hammath near the Sea of Galilee (Joshua 19:35). The name, meaning “warm” or “hot spring,” likely reflects a nearby thermal spring, a natural feature found along both stretches of coast and lakeshore in the region.

name: Cherub
dictNote: Plural cherubim, the name of certain symbolical figures frequently mentioned in Scripture. They are first mentioned in connection with the expulsion of our first parents from Eden (Gen. 3:24). There is no intimation given of their shape or form. They are next mentioned when Moses was commanded to provide furniture for the tabernacle (Ex. 25:17-20; 26:1, 31). God promised to commune with Moses “from between the cherubim” (25:22). This expression was afterwards used to denote the Divine abode and presence (Num. 7:89; 1 Sam. 4:4; Isa. 37:16; Ps. 80:1; 99:1). In Ezekiel’s vision (10:1-20) they appear as living creatures supporting the throne of God. From Ezekiel’s description of them (1;10; 41:18, 19), they appear to have been compound figures, unlike any real object in nature; artificial images possessing the features and properties of several animals. Two cherubim were placed on the mercy-seat of the ark; two of colossal size overshadowed it in Solomon’s temple. Ezekiel (1:4-14) speaks of four; and this number of “living creatures” is mentioned in Rev. 4:6. Those on the ark are called the “cherubim of glory” (Heb. 9:5), i.e., of the Shechinah, or cloud of glory, for on them the visible glory of God rested. They were placed one at each end of the mercy-seat, with wings stretched upward, and their faces “toward each other and toward the mercy-seat.” They were anointed with holy oil, like the ark itself and the other sacred furniture. The cherubim were symbolical. They were intended to represent spiritual existences in immediate contact with Jehovah. Some have regarded them as symbolical of the chief ruling power by which God carries on his operations in providence (Ps. 18:10). Others interpret them as having reference to the redemption of men, and as symbolizing the great rulers or ministers of the church. Many other opinions have been held regarding them which need not be referred to here. On the whole, it seems to be most satisfactory to regard the interpretation of the symbol to be variable, as is the symbol itself. Their office was, (1) on the expulsion of our first parents from Eden, to prevent all access to the tree of life; and (2) to form the throne and chariot of Jehovah in his manifestation of himself on earth. He dwelleth between and sitteth on the cherubim (1 Sam. 4:4; Ps. 80:1; Ezek. 1:26, 28).

name: Hobab
dictNote: Hobab was Moses' brother-in-law, a Kenite and relative of the Midianite priest Jethro, whose knowledge of the wilderness terrain Moses sought when Israel set out from Sinai, asking him to serve as guide (Numbers 10:29-32). Judges 4:11 uses the same relational term for him as for Moses' father-in-law, an ambiguity in the Hebrew word for in-law that has led some to identify Hobab with Jethro himself rather than as a separate individual. His descendants, the Kenites, settled among the Israelites, first near Jericho and later in the Negev around Arad (Judges 1:16).

name: Joktheel
note: Joktheel, the name of a place in Palestine, and of one in Idumaea
dictNote: Subdued by God. (1.) A city of Judah near Lachish (Josh. 15, 38). Perhaps the ruin Kutlaneh, south of Gezer. (2.) Amaziah, king of Judah, undertook a great expedition against Edom (2 Chr. 25:5-10), which was completely successful. He routed the Edomites and slew vast numbers of them. So wonderful did this victory appear to him that he acknowledged that it could have been achieved only by the special help of God, and therefore he called Selah (q.v.), their great fortress city, by the name of Joktheel (2 Kings 14:7).

name: Bamoth
note: Bamoth or Bamoth-Baal, a place East of the Jordan
dictNote: Heights, the forty-seventh station of the Israelites (Num. 21:19, 20) in the territory of the Moabites.

dictNote: “Canaanite,” more precisely rendered “Cananaean” in modern translations, is a byname for the apostle Simon, one of the Twelve, appearing in the disciple lists of Matthew 10:4 and Mark 3:18. Despite its appearance, the word does not mean a descendant of Canaan; it transliterates an Aramaic term for the Jewish nationalist movement known as the Zealots, matching Luke's designation of the same man as “Simon the Zealot” (Luke 6:15).

name: Shimath
dictNote: Shimath was an Ammonite woman whose son Jehozabad, along with an accomplice, assassinated King Joash of Judah in his bed, reportedly in revenge for Joash's earlier execution of the prophet Zechariah (2 Kings 12:21; 2 Chronicles 24:26). She is identified only through this connection to her son.

name: Sarid
dictNote: (survivor), a chief landmark of the territory of Zebulun. (Joshua 19:10,12) All that can be gathered of its position is that it lay to the west of Chislothtabor.

name: Netophah
dictNote: Distillation; dropping, a town in Judah, in the neighbourhood, probably, of Bethlehem (Neh. 7:26; 1 Chr. 2:54). Two of David’s guards were Netophathites (1 Chr. 27:13, 15). It has been identified with the ruins of Metoba, or Um Toba, to the north-east of Bethlehem.

name: Ananiah
note: Ananjah, the name of an Israelite and of a place in Palestine
dictNote: Protected by Jehovah, the name of a town in the tribe of Benjamin between Nob and Hazor (Neh. 11:32). It is probably the modern Beit Hanina, a small village 3 miles north of Jerusalem.

name: Barkos
dictNote: Barkos was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, or Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile, listed among those unable to prove their Israelite lineage through genealogical records (Ezra 2:53; Nehemiah 7:55).

name: Rimmon-parez
note: Rimmon-Perets, a place in the Desert
dictNote: A pomegranate breach, or Rimmon of the breach, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (Num. 33:19, 20).

name: Helkath
dictNote: Smoothness, a town of Asher, on the east border (Josh. 19:25; 21:31); called also Hukok (1 Chr. 6:75).

name: Joash
note: Joash, the name of two Israelites

name: Jehoaddan

secondTemple.excerpt: His mothers name was Jehoaddan , who was born at Jerusalem.

dictNote: Jehoaddan, also called Jehoaddin, was the wife of King Jehoash of Judah and the mother of his successor, King Amaziah; she is identified as a native of Jerusalem (2 Kings 14:2; 2 Chronicles 25:1). Scripture records nothing further about her, typical of the brief, formulaic queen-mother notices given for most kings of Judah.

name: Shalmaneser

secondTemple.excerpt: How Pekah died by the treachery of Hoshea ; who was a little after subdued by Shalmaneser .
How Shalmaneser took Samaria by force; and how he transplanted the ten tribes into Media; and brought the nation of the Cutheans into their countrey [in their room.] 1.

dictNote: Shalmaneser V ruled Assyria from about 727 to 722 BC, succeeding his father Tiglath-Pileser III. When King Hoshea of Israel withheld tribute and sought an alliance with Egypt, Shalmaneser invaded and besieged Samaria; the siege lasted roughly three years before the city fell (2 Kings 17:3-6; 18:9-11). Assyrian records are notably silent on his own account of the conquest, since he died around the time Samaria fell and his successor, Sargon II, claimed credit for the city's capture in his own inscriptions, a discrepancy that has long puzzled historians reconciling the biblical and Assyrian records. The Babylonian Chronicle independently confirms that a king by this name reigned briefly in this period, corroborating the biblical timeframe.

name: Jakim
note: Jakim, the name of two Israelites

secondTemple.excerpt: 24:12, the Course of Jakim , where some copies have the Course of Eliakim .

dictNote: Jakim was the priest who headed the twelfth of the twenty-four priestly divisions David organized for temple service (1 Chronicles 24:12). A separate Jakim was a Benjamite family head living in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:19-21). The King James margin at Matthew 1:11 also uses “Jakim” as an alternate rendering of Jehoiakim.

name: Chanaan
note: Chanaan (i.e. Kenaan), the early name of Palestine
dictNote: Chanaan is the King James Version's transliteration of “Canaan” as it appears in the Greek text of Acts, referring to the land promised to Abraham's descendants rather than to a person. Stephen's speech recalls God giving Israel no inheritance there before the conquest (Acts 7:11), while Paul's synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch recounts God destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan to give it to Israel (Acts 13:19).

name: Jehalellel
note: Jehallelel, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Jehalellel's name means “praise God.” One man of this name appears in the tribe of Judah's genealogy (1 Chronicles 4:16). A second Jehalellel was a Levite whose sons helped lead the purification of the temple under King Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 29:12).

name: Ahi
note: Achi, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Ahi, meaning “brother” or “my brother,” is the name of two otherwise unrelated men in Chronicles: a chief of a family within the tribe of Gad living in Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:15) and a family head within the tribe of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:34).

name: Jehdeiah
note: Jechdijah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Jehdeiah's name means “he who rejoices in the LORD.” One Jehdeiah was a Levite descended from Shubael who was assigned to a division of temple service under David (1 Chronicles 24:20). A second Jehdeiah, a Meronothite, was in charge of the donkeys used in David and Solomon's royal service (1 Chronicles 27:30).

name: Anaiah
note: Anajah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Anaiah stood at Ezra's right hand on the wooden platform built for the public reading of the law in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 8:4) and is likely the same man who later signed Nehemiah's covenant of renewed obedience to the law (Nehemiah 10:22).

name: Bedad
dictNote: Bedad was the father of Hadad, one of the early kings of Edom who defeated the Midianites in the territory of Moab (Genesis 36:35; 1 Chronicles 1:46). Nothing else is recorded of him.

dictNote: Hermes, sharing his name with the Greek messenger god, was a Roman Christian Paul greets among a list of believers in Rome at the end of his letter to the Romans (Romans 16:14). Nothing further is known of him; the shared name with the deity was common among slaves and freedmen in the Roman world and carries no religious significance for its bearer here.

name: Adriel
dictNote: Adriel, son of Barzillai the Meholathite, married Merab, Saul's elder daughter, after Saul withdrew her from his earlier promise to give her to David (1 Samuel 18:19). Their five sons were later handed over to the Gibeonites and executed as part of the reparations for Saul's earlier massacre of Gibeonite lives (2 Samuel 21:8-9); a textual difficulty in that passage names Michal rather than Merab as the mother, which most interpreters resolve either as scribal confusion between the two sisters or as Michal having raised her sister's sons.

name: Maher-sha-lal-bash-baz
note: Maher-Shalal-Chash-Baz; the symbolical name of the son of Isaiah
dictNote: Maher-shalal-hash-baz, meaning “quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil,” was the son of the prophet Isaiah, given this deliberately ominous name as a sign to King Ahaz that Assyria would plunder Damascus and Samaria before the child could say “father” or “mother” (Isaiah 8:1-4). Isaiah had the name publicly recorded on a large tablet before the boy's birth, witnessed by two reliable men, underscoring the prophecy's certainty. The prediction was fulfilled within a few years when Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered Damascus and stripped Israel of territory.

name: Bigthan
note: Bigthan or Bigthana, a eunuch of Xerxes

secondTemple.excerpt: Some time after this [two eunuchs] Bigthan and Teresh plotted against the King; and Barnabazus, the servant of one of the eunuchs, being by birth a Jew, was acquainted with their conspiracy, and discovered it to the Queen’s uncle.

dictNote: Bigthan, also spelled Bigthana, was one of two eunuchs who guarded the entrance to King Ahasuerus's chambers and conspired with a colleague, Teresh, to assassinate the king. Mordecai uncovered the plot and reported it, leading to the conspirators' execution by hanging, an act recorded in the palace chronicles that later proved crucial to Mordecai's own fortunes (Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-3).

name: Arvadite

dictNote: [Arvad]

name: Jahleel

secondTemple.excerpt: Zebulon and his sons; and these are the names of his sons: Sered, and Elon, and Jahleel--four.

dictNote: Jahleel was the third son of Zebulun and the ancestral head of the Jahleelite clan within that tribe (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26).

name: Gederah
note: (with the article) Gederah, a place in Palestine
dictNote: The fortress; a fortified place, a town in the plain (shephelah) of Judah (Josh. 15:36). This is a very common Canaanite and Phoenician name. It is the feminine form of Geder (12:13); the plural form is Gederoth (15:41). This place has by some been identified with Jedireh, a ruin 9 miles from Lydda, toward Eleutheropolis, and 4 miles north of Sur’ah (Zorah), in the valley of Elah.

name: Ebronah
dictNote: Passage, one of the stations of the Israelites in their wanderings (Num. 33:34, 35). It was near Ezion-geber.

name: Naptuhim
dictNote: The Naphtuhim were one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, or Egypt, listed in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11), representing an ethnic or tribal group associated with ancient Egypt rather than a single individual. Their precise historical identification is uncertain; proposals have linked them to Lower Egypt or the Nile Delta region, but no scholarly consensus exists.

name: Elipheleh
dictNote: Elipheleh was one of the Levite gatekeepers and musicians appointed to play the harp “on the Sheminith” when David brought the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18, 21). The term “Sheminith” likely designates a musical instrument, tuning, or octave register, though its precise meaning is uncertain.

dictNote: This form of “Greek” specifically denotes a Greek woman, and is used of the Syrophoenician woman who asked Jesus to heal her daughter, identified by Mark as “a Greek, a Syrophoenician by nation” (Mark 7:26), meaning a Gentile rather than an ethnic Greek by descent. It is also used of the “honourable women” among the Greeks in Berea who believed Paul's message alongside many Jews (Acts 17:12).

name: Kedemah
dictNote: Kedemah was the youngest of the twelve sons of Ishmael, listed among the tribal chiefs whose descendants became the Ishmaelite peoples of the Arabian desert (Genesis 25:15-16). His name, meaning “eastward,” fits the pattern of Ishmael's sons settling in the region east of Canaan. Nothing else is recorded about him individually.

name: Chushan-rishathayim
dictNote: Chushan-rishathayim was a king of Aram-naharaim (Mesopotamia) whom God allowed to oppress Israel for eight years during the period of the judges, the first of the foreign oppressions recorded in Judges. Israel cried out to the LORD, who raised up Othniel, Caleb's younger kinsman, to defeat him and secure forty years of peace (Judges 3:8-11). His title, which means something like “doubly wicked Cushan,” may be a Hebrew wordplay on his actual name rather than his given name.

name: Bealoth

secondTemple.excerpt: And he removed from thence and went towards the south,  and he came to Hebron, and Hebron was built at, that time, and he dwelt there two years, and he went (thence) into the land of the south, to Bealoth  and there was a famine in the land.

dictNote: Citizens, a town in the extreme south of Judah (Josh. 15:24); probably the same as Baalath-beer (19:8). In 1 Kings 4:16, the Authorized Version has “in Aloth,” the Revised Version “Bealoth.”

name: Jehieli
note: a Jechielite or descendant of Jechiel
dictNote: Jehieli was a Gershonite Levite descended from Ladan, head of a family placed in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD under David (1 Chronicles 26:21-22). He and his brother Zetham administered the dedicated gifts and spoils brought in for the temple's future construction. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Heldai
note: Cheldai, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men in the Old Testament carry this name. The first, a Netophathite also called Heleb or Heled, was one of David's thirty mighty men and commanded the army division on duty in the twelfth month (2 Samuel 23:29; 1 Chronicles 27:15). The second was one of a group of exiles who returned from Babylon bringing gold and silver, from which the prophet Zechariah was told to make a crown for Joshua the high priest as a sign of the coming Messianic king-priest (Zechariah 6:10-11).

name: Jaasiel
dictNote: This name is attached to two men in Chronicles. Jasiel the Mesobaite appears among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:47), while Jaasiel son of Abner served as chief officer over the tribe of Benjamin under David's administrative system (1 Chronicles 27:21). Whether these are the same man is not stated in the text.

name: Evil-merodach
dictNote: Evil-merodach, known in Babylonian records as Amel-Marduk, succeeded his father Nebuchadnezzar II as king of Babylon around 562 BC. In the year he began to reign he released the exiled Judean king Jehoiachin from prison, showed him favor, and gave him a regular place at the royal table for the rest of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30; Jeremiah 52:31-34). Babylonian sources confirm him as Nebuchadnezzar's son and successor, though he reigned only about two years before being overthrown.

name: Cozbi

secondTemple.excerpt: Even Zimri, the head of the tribe of Simeon, accompanied with Cozbi, a Midianitish women, who was the daughter of Sur; a man of authority in that countrey: and being desired by his wife to disregard the laws of Moses, and to follow those she was used to, he complied with her: and this b

dictNote: Cozbi was a Midianite woman, daughter of a tribal chief named Zur, who was killed along with the Israelite man Zimri by Phinehas the priest for their open immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 25:6-18). The incident, and the plague that followed it, was remembered afterward as a warning against intermarriage that led Israel into idolatry.

name: Jabneel
note: Jabneel, the name of two places in Palestine
dictNote: Jabneel is the name of two towns in the conquest narratives, not a person. One marked the northwestern border of Judah near the coast, later known as Jabneh or Jamnia (Joshua 15:11); the other lay on the boundary of Naphtali in the north (Joshua 19:33). The coastal Jabneh later became a notable Jewish town, and its walls were torn down by King Uzziah of Judah (2 Chronicles 26:6).

name: Joha
note: Jocha, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Joha appear in Chronicles. One was a Benjamite, son of Beriah, listed among the heads of families living in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:16). The other, called the Tizite, was one of David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:45). Nothing else distinguishes them.

name: Ashnah
note: Ashnah, the name of two places in Palestine
dictNote: Ashnah is the name of two towns in the lowland (Shephelah) territory of Judah, not a person. One is listed near Zorah and Eshtaol (Joshua 15:33), and the other appears later in the same tribal boundary list near Nezib and Keilah (Joshua 15:43). Their exact sites are uncertain today.

name: Anab
dictNote: Grape-town, one of the cities in the mountains of Judah, from which Joshua expelled the Anakim (Josh. 11:21; 15:50). It still retains its ancient name. It lies among the hills, 10 miles south-south-west of Hebron.

name: Beeri
note: Beeri, the name of a Hittite and of an Israelite
dictNote: Two Old Testament men bear this name. The first was a Hittite whose daughter Judith became one of Esau's wives, a marriage that grieved his parents Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 26:34-35). The second was the father of the prophet Hosea, known only from the opening verse of Hosea's book (Hosea 1:1).

name: Eshton
dictNote: Eshton appears in the genealogy of Judah as a descendant of Chelub, credited with fathering Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash (1 Chronicles 4:11-12). The list preserves little more than these family names, likely tied to towns or clans that no longer survive.

name: Jerusha

secondTemple.excerpt: 759.] Now Jotham, the son of Uzziah, reigned over the tribe of Judah in Jerusalem: being a citizen thereof by his mother, whose name was Jerusha .

dictNote: Jerusha, daughter of Zadok, was the wife of King Uzziah of Judah and mother of his successor Jotham (2 Kings 15:33; 2 Chronicles 27:1). Nothing more is recorded of her beyond this genealogical notice.

name: Meshillemoth
dictNote: Two men carry this name. The first was the father of Berechiah, an Ephraimite chief who, along with other leaders, opposed enslaving Judean captives taken in war and insisted they be fed, clothed, and sent home (2 Chronicles 28:9-15). The second was an ancestor of Amashsai, a priest who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (Nehemiah 11:13).

name: Jareb
note: Jareb, a symbolical name for Assyria
dictNote: Jareb is not a personal name but an obscure Hebrew phrase, traditionally rendered “King Jareb,” that appears twice in Hosea describing Israel's futile appeals to Assyria for help (Hosea 5:13; 10:6). Most modern scholars read it as an epithet for the Assyrian king, something like “a king who contends” or “the great king,” rather than a proper name, so it likely refers to Tiglath-pileser III or the Assyrian monarchy in general rather than to a specific named individual.

name: Sosthenes
note: of safe strength; Sosthenes, a Christian
dictNote: Sosthenes was the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth who was seized and beaten in front of the Roman proconsul Gallio's judgment seat after the Jewish community's case against Paul was dismissed (Acts 18:12-17). dictNote: Nisan is not a person but the first month of the Hebrew religious calendar, corresponding roughly to March-April, also called Abib in earlier texts. It is named in Nehemiah as the month in which he approached King Artaxerxes about rebuilding Jerusalem's walls (Nehemiah 2:1), and in Esther as the month in which Haman cast lots to fix the date for the destruction of the Jews (Esther 3:7).

name: Hariph
note: Chariph, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Hariph was the ancestral head of a family, also called Jorah, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel; his name appears both among the list of returnees and among those who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 7:24; 10:19; compare Ezra 2:18).

name: Bath-shua
dictNote: Bath-shua, meaning “daughter of Shua,” is used of two different women in Chronicles. It names the Canaanite wife of Judah, mother of Er, Onan, and Shelah, elsewhere called simply “the daughter of Shua” (1 Chronicles 2:3; compare Genesis 38:2). It is also used as a variant of Bathsheba, wife of David and mother of Solomon (1 Chronicles 3:5).

name: Sheshbazzar
dictNote: O sun-god, defend the lord! (Ezra 1:8, 11), probably another name for Zerubbabel (q.v.), Ezra 2:2; Hag. 1:12, 14; Zech. 4:6, 10.

name: Sheshbazzar
dictNote: Sheshbazzar was a prince of Judah appointed governor by King Cyrus of Persia, entrusted with the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and commissioned to lead the first group of returning exiles and lay the foundation of the rebuilt temple (Ezra 1:8, 11; 5:14-16). Some scholars identify him with Zerubbabel, though the text treats them as though performing overlapping roles rather than stating they are the same man.

name: Gazathite
note: an Azzathite or inhabitant of Azzah

name: Keros
dictNote: Keros was the ancestral head of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47).

name: Eldad
dictNote: Eldad was one of the seventy elders Moses appointed to help bear the burden of leading Israel. When the Spirit rested on the elders at the tent of meeting, Eldad and his companion Medad, who had remained in the camp, also prophesied there; when Joshua urged Moses to stop them, Moses responded by wishing that all the LORD's people were prophets (Numbers 11:24-29).

name: Zelah
dictNote: Slope; side, a town in Benjamin, where Saul and his son Jonathan were buried (2 Sam. 21:14). It was probably Saul’s birthplace.

name: Parbar
note: Parbar or Parvar, a quarter of Jerusalem
dictNote: Parbar is not a person but a structure or precinct on the west side of the temple complex, apparently a colonnade or open court, mentioned in connection with gatekeepers assigned there (1 Chronicles 26:18) and possibly the same area where wicked King Manasseh had placed horses dedicated to the sun (2 Kings 23:11).

name: Ezbon

dictNote: Two men are named Ezbon in the genealogies. One was a son of Gad, also called Ozni, who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family (Genesis 46:16; compare Numbers 26:16). The other was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, listed as a head of a family in that tribe (1 Chronicles 7:7).

name: Jekamiah
note: Jekamjah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Jekamiah appear in the genealogies of Judah. One descended from Sheshan through his daughter's marriage to an Egyptian servant, in the line of Ahlai (1 Chronicles 2:35-41). The other was a son of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), born to him in captivity in Babylon (1 Chronicles 3:18).

Strangers from this province were at Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), and to “strangers scattered throughout Pontus,” among others, Peter addresses his first epistle (1 Pet. 1:1). It was evidently the resort of many Jews of the Dispersion. Aquila was a native of Pontus (Acts 18:2).

note: pointed; (used with the article as a proper name) Senuah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Hasenuah, whose Hebrew name includes the definite article (“the Senuah”), was an ancestor of a Benjamite family that resettled in Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:7; Nehemiah 11:9).

name: Amok
dictNote: Amok was a priest who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and became head of a priestly family; his descendant Eber served as head of that family in the days of the high priest Joiakim (Nehemiah 12:7, 20).

name: Pergamos
note: fortified; Pergamus, a place in Asia Minor
dictNote: The chief city of Mysia, in Asia Minor. One of the “seven churches” was planted here (Rev. 1:11; 2:17). It was noted for its wickedness, insomuch that our Lord says “Satan’s seat” was there. The church of Pergamos was rebuked for swerving from the truth and embracing the doctrines of Balaam and the Nicolaitanes. Antipas, Christ’s “faithful martyr,” here sealed his testimony with his blood. This city stood on the banks of the river Caicus, about 20 miles from the sea. It is now called Bergama, and has a population of some twenty thousand, of whom about two thousand profess to be Christians. Parchment (q.v.) was first made here, and was called by the Greeks pergamene, from the name of the city.

name: Bochim
dictNote: Weepers, a place where the angel of the Lord reproved the Israelites for entering into a league with the people of the land. This caused them bitterly to weep, and hence the name of the place (Judg. 2:1, 5). It lay probably at the head of one of the valleys between Gilgal and Shiloh.

name: Mibzar
dictNote: Mibzar, meaning “fortress,” was listed among the chiefs, or “dukes,” of Edom descended from Esau (Genesis 36:42; 1 Chronicles 1:53). Like several other Edomite chief names in this list, it probably doubles as the name of a clan territory or stronghold rather than referring only to an individual.

name: Ozias
dictNote: Ozias is the Greek New Testament spelling of Uzziah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:8-9), where he is listed as the son of Joram and ancestor of Christ. In the Old Testament, Uzziah reigned as king of Judah for over fifty years and was struck with leprosy after presumptuously burning incense in the temple, a priestly duty reserved for Aaron's line.

name: Shaalbonite
note: a Shaalbonite or inhabitant of Shaalbin

name: Hymenaeus
dictNote: Hymenaeus was a man in the early church, probably at Ephesus, whom Paul names twice as an example of shipwrecked faith. In 1 Timothy 1:20 Paul says he handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan for blasphemy, and in 2 Timothy 2:17-18 he links Hymenaeus with Philetus for teaching that the resurrection had already taken place, a claim Paul says overturned the faith of some believers.

name: Tanhumeth
dictNote: Tanhumeth was a Netophathite whose son Seraiah was among the army captains who submitted to Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, after the fall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8).

name: Chelub
note: Kelub, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Chelub is a name given to two different men in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. One was the brother of Shuhah and father of Mehir, in the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:11). The other was the father of Ezri, who oversaw the farm workers in David's administration (1 Chronicles 27:26).

name: Sered

dictNote: Sered was a son of Zebulun who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and became the ancestor of the clan of the Seredites (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26).

name: Anath

dictNote: Anath was the father of Shamgar, one of Israel's early judges who struck down six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (Judges 3:31; 5:6). The name is shared with the Canaanite warrior goddess Anat, but in these verses it functions as a personal or place name for Shamgar's father.

name: Gadi
dictNote: Gadi was the father of Menahem, a king of Israel who seized the throne by assassinating Shallum and ruled with notable brutality (2 Kings 15:14, 17).

name: Nogah
dictNote: Nogah was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem after David became king there, listed among his children by unnamed wives (1 Chronicles 3:7; 14:6).

dictNote: Dorcas, called Tabitha in Aramaic, was a Christian woman at Joppa remembered for her charity; she made clothing for the widows in her care. When she died, the disciples sent for Peter, who raised her back to life, and the miracle led many in Joppa to believe (Acts 9:36-41).

name: Iram

name: Sia
note: Sia or Siaha, one of the Nethinim
dictNote: Sia headed a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel to serve at the rebuilt temple (Ezra 2:44; Nehemiah 7:47, where the name appears as Siaha).

name: Joshbekashah
dictNote: Joshbekashah was a son of Heman, David's seer, and headed the seventeenth of the twenty-four courses of temple musicians David organized for worship (1 Chronicles 25:4, 24).

name: Zetham
dictNote: Zetham was a Levite of the family of Ladan who served among those David put in charge of the temple treasuries (1 Chronicles 23:8; 26:22).

name: Habakkuk
dictNote: Habakkuk was a prophet who openly questioned God, asking why he tolerated Judah's injustice and then, when told Babylon would be the instrument of judgment, asking how God could use a nation even more wicked than Judah to punish it. The book records God's answer and ends with Habakkuk choosing to trust and even rejoice in God despite having no resolution to his questions, famously declaring that the righteous will live by faith, a line Paul later builds an entire theology of salvation around.

name: Mikneiah
dictNote: Mikneiah was a Levite of the second rank whom David appointed as a gatekeeper and musician, playing the harp in the choir that accompanied the ark's procession to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:18, 21).

name: Beth-palet
dictNote: (house of flight), a town among those in the extreme south of Judah, named in (Joshua 15:27)

name: Jada
dictNote: Jada was a son of Onam and brother of Shammai, listed in the genealogy of the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah's descendants (1 Chronicles 2:28, 32).

name: Medan

dictNote: Medan was a son of Abraham by his concubine Keturah and became the ancestor of an Arabian tribe grouped with Midian and other Keturah clans east of Canaan (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32).

name: Gederoth
dictNote: (sheepfolds), a town in the low country of Judah. (Joshua 15:41; 2 Chronicles 28:18)

name: Zelotes
note: a Zealot, i.e. (specially) partisan for Jewish political independence
dictNote: Zelotes, meaning the Zealot, is the epithet attached to the apostle Simon in Luke's lists of the twelve, distinguishing him from Simon Peter (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). It likely reflects either former ties to the Jewish Zealot movement, which sought armed resistance to Roman rule, or simply a zealous temperament; Matthew and Mark instead call him Simon the Canaanite, a Semitic term with the same meaning.

name: Ziza
note: Ziza, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Ziza appear in Chronicles. The first was a Simeonite prince whose clan drove out the peaceful people of Gedor and settled their land during Hezekiah's reign (1 Chronicles 4:37-43). The second was a son born to King Rehoboam of Judah by his favored wife Maachah (2 Chronicles 11:20-21).

name: Mahalath
note: Machalath, the name of an Ishmaelitess and of an Israelitess

secondTemple.excerpt: For in the days when Jacob went to Mesopotamia, Esau took to himself a wife Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, and he gathered together all the flocks of his father and his wives, and went up and dwelt on Mount Seir, and left Isaac his father at the Well of the Oath alone.  19.

dictNote: Two women named Mahalath appear in the genealogies. One was a daughter of Ishmael whom Esau married, apparently also called Bashemath, in an attempt to please his parents after his earlier marriages to Canaanite women displeased them (Genesis 28:9; 36:3). The other was a granddaughter of David, daughter of Jerimoth, who became one of Rehoboam's wives (2 Chronicles 11:18).

name: Mahalath
note: 'Machalath', probably the title (initial word) of a popular song

secondTemple.excerpt: For in the days when Jacob went to Mesopotamia, Esau took to himself a wife Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, and he gathered together all the flocks of his father and his wives, and went up and dwelt on Mount Seir, and left Isaac his father at the Well of the Oath alone.  19.

dictNote: Mahalath here is not a person but a musical or liturgical term in the headings of Psalms 53 and 88, both of which are set "upon Mahalath." Its exact meaning is uncertain; suggestions include a tune name, a wind instrument, or a word related to sickness or suffering fitting the psalms' somber content, but no consensus survives from antiquity.

name: Rithmah
note: Rithmah, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Wild broom, a station in the wilderness (Num. 33:18, 19), the “broom valley,” or “valley of broombushes,” the place apparently of the original encampment of Israel, near Kadesh.

name: Harbona
note: Charbona or Charbonah, a eunuch of Xerxes

secondTemple.excerpt: 9 [ The eunuch Sabuchadas :] Harbonah, Heb.

dictNote: Harbona was one of seven eunuchs who served King Ahasuerus of Persia and was sent to summon Queen Vashti to the king's banquet (Esther 1:10). He reappears at the story's climax, pointing out to the king the gallows Haman had built for Mordecai, which Haman was then hanged on himself (Esther 7:9).

name: Tibni

secondTemple.excerpt: Upon which the people of Israel were presently divided, and part of them would have Tibni to be king, and part Omri; but when those that were for Omri's ruling had beaten Tibni, Omri reigned over all the multitude.

dictNote: Tibni son of Ginath was a rival claimant to the throne of Israel after the death of Zimri, backed by roughly half the people for four years while Omri's faction contended against him. Omri eventually prevailed and Tibni died, leaving Omri sole king (1 Kings 16:21-22).

dictNote: Jupiter, known to the Greeks as Zeus, was the chief god of the Greco-Roman pantheon, ruler of the sky and the other gods. At Lystra the crowd, astonished when Paul healed a man lame from birth, hailed Barnabas as Jupiter and Paul as Mercury and the local priest of Jupiter, whose temple stood before the city, brought oxen to sacrifice to them until Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes and stopped the crowd (Acts 14:11-18).

name: Melchi
note: Melchi (i.e. Malki), the name of two Israelites

secondTemple.excerpt: He had three male children, Jonathan, and Ishui, and Melchi-shua; with Merab and Michal his daughters.

dictNote: Melchi is the name of two different ancestors in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, both counted through the line of Mary or Joseph's legal descent rather than Matthew's. One Melchi is the father of Neri and stands roughly at the time of the Babylonian exile (Luke 3:27-28); the other is much closer to Jesus, the father of Levi and son of Janna (Luke 3:24).

name: Perida
note: Peruda or Perida, one of 'Solomon's servants'
dictNote: Perida, also spelled Peruda, headed a family of servants of Solomon whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57).

name: Amana
dictNote: Perennial. (1.) The Hebrew margin of 2 Kings 5:12 gives this as another reading of Abana (q.v.), a stream near Damascus. (2.) A mountain (Cant. 4:8), probably the southern summit of Anti-Libanus, at the base of which are the sources of the Abana.

name: Hul
note: Chul, a son of Aram; also the region settled by him
dictNote: Circle, the second son of Aram (Gen. 10:23), and grandson of Shem.

name: Hotham
note: Chotham, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Hotham was a chief of the tribe of Asher, son of Heber of the clan of Beriah (1 Chronicles 7:32). A second Hotham, the Aroerite, is listed among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:44).

name: Beth-baal-meon
dictNote: (house of Baalmeon), a place in the possessions of Reuben, on the downs (Authorized Version “plain”) east of the Jordan. (Joshua 13:17) At the Israelites’ first approach is name was BAAL-MEON, (Numbers 32:38) or, in its contracted form, BEON (Numbers 32:3) to which the Beth was possibly a Hebrew addition. Later it would seem to have come into possession of Moab, and to be known either as Beth-meon, (Jeremiah 48:23) or Baal-meon. (Ezekiel 25:9) The name is still attached to a ruined place of considerable size a short distance to the southwest of Hesban, and bearing the name of “the fortress of Mi’un, ” or Makin .

name: Morashthite
note: a Morashtite or inhabitant of Moresheth-Gath

name: Ishmaiah
note: Jishmajah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Ishmaiah appear in Chronicles. One was a Gibeonite warrior who joined David's forces at Ziklag while David was still fleeing Saul, noted as a leading man among the thirty mighty men (1 Chronicles 12:4). The other, son of Obadiah, served as chief officer over the tribe of Zebulun under David (1 Chronicles 27:19).

name: Assos
note: Assus, a city of Asia MInor
dictNote: A sea-port town of Proconsular Asia, in the district of Mysia, on the north shore of the Gulf of Adramyttium. Paul came hither on foot along the Roman road from Troas (Acts 20:13, 14), a distance of 20 miles. It was about 30 miles distant from Troas by sea. The island of Lesbos lay opposite it, about 7 miles distant.

name: Kolaiah
note: Kolajah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Kolaiah was the father of the false prophet Ahab, who along with Zedekiah prophesied lies to the exiles in Babylon and was condemned by Jeremiah; Nebuchadnezzar had both men roasted in the fire as a warning (Jeremiah 29:21-22). A separate Kolaiah was a Benjamite ancestor of one of the returned exiles who resettled Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:7).

name: Kehelathah
note: Kehelathah, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Assembly, one of the stations of the Israelites in the desert (Num. 33:22, 23).

name: Hadad

ild of the stock of the Edomites, and of the blood royal; and when Joab, the captain of David's host, laid waste the land of Edom, and destroyed all that were men grown, and able to bear arms, for six months' time, this Hadad fled away, and came to Pharaoh the king of Egypt, who received him kindly, and assigned him a house to dwell in, and a country to supply him with food; and when he was grown up he loved him exceedingly, insomuch that he

(22) Since the beginning of Solomon's evil life and adversity was the time when Hadad or Ader, who was born at least twenty or thirty years before Solomon came to the crown, in the days of David, began to give him disturbance, this implies that Solomon's evil life began early, and continued very long, wh

dictNote: Hadad was a common name among Edomite kings and also the name of an Edomite prince who fled to Egypt as a child when David's forces conquered Edom, later returning as an adversary who troubled Solomon's reign.

name: Hezro
dictNote: Hezro the Carmelite was one of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters who distinguished themselves in David's service (2 Samuel 23:35; 1 Chronicles 11:37).

name: Telassar
dictNote: Or Thelasar, (Isa. 37:12; 2 Kings 19:12), a province in the south-east of Assyria, probably in Babylonia. Some have identified it with Tel Afer, a place in Mesopotamia, some 30 miles from Sinjar.

name: Gahar
dictNote: Gahar headed a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:47; Nehemiah 7:49).

name: Amramite
note: an Amramite or descendant of Amram

name: Maaziah
note: Maazjah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Maaziah headed the twenty-fourth and last of the priestly divisions David organized for temple service (1 Chronicles 24:18). A priest by the same name later sealed Nehemiah's covenant to keep God's law after the exile (Nehemiah 10:8).

name: Sinite
note: a Sinite, or descendant of one of the sons of Canaan
dictNote: An inhabitant of Sin, near Arka (Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15). (See ARKITE.)

name: Chorazin
dictNote: Named along with Bethsaida and Capernaum as one of the cities in which our Lord’s “mighty works” were done, and which was doomed to woe because of signal privileges neglected (Matt. 11:21; Luke 10:13). It has been identified by general consent with the modern Kerazeh, about 2 1/2 miles up the Wady Kerazeh from Capernaum; i.e., Tell Hum.

name: Pithon
dictNote: Pithon was a son of Micah and grandson of Mephibosheth, in the genealogy preserving the line of King Saul through his son Jonathan (1 Chronicles 8:35; 9:41).

name: Hatipha
dictNote: Hatipha headed a family among the Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:54; Nehemiah 7:56).

name: Dinhaban
dictNote: This entry's name is a data variant of Dinhabah, which is a place, not a person: the capital city of Bela son of Beor, the first king listed in Edom's roster of early rulers (Genesis 36:32; 1 Chronicles 1:43). Its location is unknown, though it lay somewhere in the region later called Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea.

name: Mede
note: a Madian or native of Madai

dictNote: Mede is not an individual but an ethnic designation for an inhabitant of Media, the ancient kingdom in what is now northwestern Iran. The Medes allied with Babylon to topple Assyria and later merged with Persia under Cyrus to form the Medo-Persian Empire that conquered Babylon; Daniel refers to their laws and kings, and Medes are among the nations represented at Pentecost in Acts 2:9.

name: Rab-mag
dictNote: Rab-mag is not a personal name but a Babylonian court title, roughly chief of the magi or chief soothsayer, held by Nergal-sharezer, one of the officials Nebuchadnezzar sent to oversee the fall of Jerusalem and the treatment of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 39:3, 13).

name: Hirah
dictNote: Hirah was an Adullamite and close friend of Judah, present when Judah married a Canaanite woman and later sent by Judah to deliver a goat to Tamar in payment for what he did not realize was a disguised encounter with his own daughter-in-law (Genesis 38:1, 12, 20).

name: Calcol

secondTemple.excerpt: He also excelled and distinguished himself in wisdom above those who were most eminent among the Hebrews at that time for shrewdness; those I mean were Ethan, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol.

dictNote: Calcol was renowned for wisdom among the sons of Zerah, or possibly of Mahol, and is named alongside Ethan, Heman, and Darda as men whose wisdom Solomon's surpassed (1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 2:6).

name: Aser

secondTemple.excerpt: The tribe of Aser had that part which was called the Valley ; for such it was: and all that part which lay over against Sidon.
Gad and Aser were the sons of Zilpha, who was the handmaid of Lea.

dictNote: Aser is the Greek New Testament form of Asher, Jacob's eighth son and ancestor of the tribe of Asher. The name appears identifying the prophetess Anna's tribal descent (Luke 2:36) and among the twelve tribes listed as sealed in Revelation 7:6.

name: Sheleph
dictNote: Sheleph was a son of Joktan and became the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, one of many Joktanite peoples listed as settling the Arabian peninsula (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20).

name: Berea

secondTemple.excerpt: And then the forementioned Antiochus, and Lysias the general of his army, deprived Onias, who was also named Menelaus , of the High Priesthood, and slew him at Berea; and driving away the son [of Onias the third,] put Jacimus into the place of the High Priest.
So the king sent Menelaus to Berea, a city of Syria, and there had him put to death, when he had been high priest ten years.
But when Demetrius was departed out of Judea, he went to Berea, and besieged his brother Philip, having with him ten thousand footmen, and a thousand horsemen.

dictNote: A city of Macedonia to which Paul with Silas and Timotheus went when persecuted at Thessalonica (Acts 17:10, 13), and from which also he was compelled to withdraw, when he fled to the sea-coast and thence sailed to Athens (14, 15). Sopater, one of Paul’s companions belonged to this city, and his conversion probably took place at this time (Acts 20:4). It is now called Verria.

name: Jezaniah

secondTemple.excerpt: Now the rulers that were over them were Johanan, the son of Kareah; and Jezaniah, and Seraiah, and others beside them.

dictNote: Jezaniah, son of Hoshaiah the Maachathite, commanded one of the bands of Judean soldiers who had escaped into the countryside during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. He submitted to Gedaliah, the governor Babylon installed over Judah, but after Gedaliah's assassination he was among the leaders who, against Jeremiah's warning, forced the remaining Judeans to flee to Egypt (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8; 42:1; 43:2).

name: Esrom

secondTemple.excerpt: Judas had three sons - Sala, Phares, Zerah; and by Phares two grandchildren, Esrom and Amar.

dictNote: Esrom is the Greek New Testament form of Hezron, a grandson of Judah through Perez, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in both Matthew's and Luke's genealogies (Matthew 1:3; Luke 3:33).

name: Manasses

secondTemple.excerpt: Rachel had two sons, the one of whom, Joseph, had two sons also, Manasses and Ephraim.
