dictNote: Manasses is the Greek New Testament form of Manasseh and refers to two different things. In Matthew's genealogy it names the notorious king of Judah, ancestor of Jesus, who reigned longer than any other Judean king and led the nation into idolatry (Matthew 1:10). In Revelation it instead names the tribe descended from Joseph's son Manasseh, listed among the twelve tribes sealed by God (Revelation 7:6).

name: Ard
note: Ard, the name of two Israelites

secondTemple.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

dictNote: Ard was a grandson of Benjamin, son of Bela, and became the ancestor of the clan of the Ardites; he is called Addar in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:3 (Genesis 46:21; Numbers 26:40).

name: Orpah

secondTemple.excerpt: wife, and the children that were born to him by her, Chilion and Mahlon; and removed his habitation into the land of Moab: and upon the happy prosperity of his affairs there, he took for his sons wives of the Moabites, Orpah for Chilion and Ruth for Mahlon.

dictNote: Orpah was a Moabite woman married to Chilion, one of Naomi's sons, and sister-in-law to Ruth. When Naomi decided to return to Bethlehem after her husband and sons died, Orpah wept and, after Naomi's urging, chose to stay in Moab with her own people, unlike Ruth who famously clung to Naomi (Ruth 1:4-14).

name: Uphaz
dictNote: Probably another name for Ophir (Jer. 10:9). Some, however, regard it as the name of an Indian colony in Yemen, southern Arabia; others as a place on or near the river Hyphasis (now the Ghana), the south-eastern limit of the Punjaub.

name: Merib-baal
note: quarreller of Baal, Merib-Baal, an epithet of Gideon
dictNote: Merib-baal is the name given in the Chronicles genealogies to Jonathan's son, elsewhere called Mephibosheth in the books of Samuel (1 Chronicles 8:34; 9:40; compare 2 Samuel 4:4). The change from Baal-based names to substitutes like Bosheth, meaning shame, likely reflects later discomfort with the divine title Baal, lord, once used more neutrally in personal names.

name: Nobah
note: Nobach, the name of an Israelite, and of a place East of the Jordan
dictNote: Howling. (1.) Num. 32:42. (2.) The name given to Kenath (q.v.) by Nobah when he conquered it. It was on the east of Gilead (Judg. 8:11).

name: Hiddekel
dictNote: Called by the Accadians id Idikla; i.e., “the river of Idikla”, the third of the four rivers of Paradise (Gen. 2:14). Gesenius interprets the word as meaning “the rapid Tigris.” The Tigris rises in the mountains of Armenia, 15 miles south of the source of the Euphrates, which, after pursuing a south-east course, it joins at Kurnah, about 50 miles above Bassorah. Its whole length is about 1,150 miles.

name: Baal-perazim
dictNote: Baal having rents, bursts, or destructions, the scene of a victory gained by David over the Philistines (2 Sam. 5:20; 1 Chr. 14:11). Called Mount Perazim (Isa. 28:21). It was near the valley of Rephaim, west of Jerusalem. Identified with the modern Jebel Aly.

name: Halak
dictNote: Smooth; bald, a hill at the southern extremity of Canaan (Josh. 11:17). It is referred to as if it were a landmark in that direction, being prominent and conspicuous from a distance. It has by some been identified with the modern Jebel el-Madura, on the south frontier of Judah, between the south end of the Dead Sea and the Wady Gaian.

name: Arkite
note: an Arkite or inhabitant of Erek
dictNote: (Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15), a designation of certain descendants from the Phoenicians or Sidonians, the inhabitants of Arka, 12 miles north of Tripoli, opposite the northern extremity of Lebanon.

name: Azaliah
dictNote: Azaliah was the father of Shaphan, the royal scribe who read the newly discovered Book of the Law to King Josiah and helped spark Josiah's religious reforms (2 Kings 22:3; 2 Chronicles 34:8).

name: Zalmonah
note: Tsalmonah, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Shady, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (Num. 33:41, 42).

name: Juttah
note: Juttah (or Jutah), a place in Palestine
dictNote: Extended, a Levitical city in the mountains or hill-country of Judah (Josh. 15:55; 21:16). Its modern name is Yutta, a place about 5 1/2 miles south of Hebron. It is supposed to have been the residence of Zacharias and Elisabeth, and the birthplace of John the Baptist, and on this account is annually visited by thousands of pilgrims belonging to the Greek Church (Luke 1:39). (See MARY.)

name: Ether
dictNote: (abundance), one of the cities of Judah in the low country, the Shefelah, (Joshua 15:42) allotted to Simeon. (Joshua 19:7)

name: Sabta
note: Sabta or Sabtah, the name of a son of Cush, and the country occupied by his posterity
dictNote: Sabta, also spelled Sabtah, was a son of Cush and grandson of Ham, and became the eponymous ancestor of a people grouped with other early tribes of Arabia or northeast Africa (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9).

name: Bedan
note: Bedan, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Bedan is named among Israel's deliverers in Samuel's farewell speech, alongside Jerubbaal, Barak, and Jephthah, though his identity is uncertain since no judge by that name appears in the book of Judges; some identify him with Samson or Abdon, or take the name as a variant of Barak (1 Samuel 12:11). A different Bedan, of the tribe of Manasseh, appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:17.

name: Ginath
dictNote: Ginath was the father of Tibni, the man whose supporters contended for the throne of Israel against Omri for four years before Omri prevailed (1 Kings 16:21-22).

name: Shephuphan
dictNote: Shephuphan was a son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, ancestor of the clan of the Shuphamites; the name also appears as Shupham, Shuppim, and Muppim in parallel genealogies (Numbers 26:39; 1 Chronicles 8:5).

name: Giloh
dictNote: Exile, a city in the south-west part of the hill-country of Judah (Josh. 15:51). It was the native place or residence of the traitor Ahithophel “the Gilonite” (Josh. 15:51; 2 Sam. 15:12), and where he committed suicide (17:23). It has been identified with Kurbet Jala, about 7 miles north of Hebron.

name: Amzi
dictNote: Two men named Amzi appear in postexilic records. One was a Levite ancestor of Ethan, one of the temple musicians David appointed (1 Chronicles 6:31, 44-45). The other was a priest whose descendant resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:12).

name: Naasson
dictNote: Naasson is the Greek New Testament form of Nahshon, a prince of the tribe of Judah during Israel's wilderness wanderings and brother-in-law of Aaron through his sister Elisheba. He is listed as an ancestor of Jesus in both Matthew's and Luke's genealogies (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:32).

name: Nimrim
note: Nimrim, a place East of the Jordan
dictNote: (limpid, pure), The waters of, a stream or brook within the country of Moab, which is mentioned in the denunciations of that nation by Isaiah. (Isaiah 15:6) and Jeremiah. (Jeremiah 48:34) We should perhaps look for the site of Nimrim in Moab proper, i.e. on the southeastern shoulder of the Dead Sea.

name: Hamathite
note: a Chamathite or native of Chamath

name: Hanniel
note: Channiel, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Hanniel appear in the Pentateuch and Chronicles. One was a chief of the tribe of Manasseh whom Moses appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Numbers 34:23). The other was a chief of the tribe of Asher, listed among mighty warriors and heads of families (1 Chronicles 7:39-40).

name: Binea
dictNote: Binea was a descendant of King Saul through the line of Jonathan and Mephibosheth, preserved in the genealogy of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:37; 9:43).

name: Heres
dictNote: Sun. (1.) “Mount Heres” (Judg. 1:35), Heb. Har-heres, i.e., “sun-mountain;” probably identical with Irshemesh in Josh. 19:41. (2.) Isa. 19:18, marg. (See ON.)

name: Hatita
dictNote: Hatita headed a family of temple gatekeepers whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:42; Nehemiah 7:45).

name: Hachaliah
dictNote: Hachaliah was the father of Nehemiah, the cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes who obtained leave to return to Jerusalem and rebuild its walls (Nehemiah 1:1; 10:1).

name: Shuni

secondTemple.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

dictNote: Shuni was a son of Gad who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family and became the ancestor of the clan of the Shunites (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:15).

name: Gether
note: Gether, a son of Aram, and the region settled by him
dictNote: (fear), the third in order of the sons of Aram. (Genesis 10:23) No satisfactory trace of the people sprung from this stock has been found.

name: Teresh

secondTemple.excerpt: Some time after this [two eunuchs] Bigthan and Teresh plotted against the King; and Barnabazus, the servant of one of the eunuchs, being by birth a Jew, was acquainted with their conspiracy, and discovered it to the Queen’s uncle.

dictNote: Teresh was a eunuch who guarded the entrance to the palace of the Persian king Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I. Along with a fellow guard, Bigthan, he plotted to assassinate the king, but Mordecai learned of the conspiracy and reported it, and the two men were executed. The record of Mordecai's service was later read to the king and became the turning point that led to Mordecai's promotion (Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-3).

name: Giddalti
dictNote: Giddalti was one of the sons of Heman, a Levite musician in David's court. He headed one of the twenty-four divisions of temple musicians organized under David to lead worship with song and instruments (1 Chronicles 25:4, 29).

name: Maaseiah

secondTemple.excerpt: And when the money was brought in, he made one Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Shaphan the Scribe, and Joab the Recorder, and Eliakim the High Priest, curators of the temple, and of the charges contributed thereto.

dictNote: Maaseiah was a common priestly and Levitical name in the Old Testament, borne by several different individuals involved in temple service, the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls under Nehemiah, and the reading of the law to the returned exiles.

name: Elamite
note: an Elamite or inhabitant of Elam

name: Ithiel
note: Ithiel, the name of an Israelite, also of a symbolical person
dictNote: Two different men bear this name in the Bible. One is listed among the Benjamite ancestors of the Jerusalem settlers who returned after the exile (Nehemiah 11:7). The other appears in the opening line of Agur's sayings in Proverbs 30:1, addressed alongside Ucal, though the Hebrew wording there is difficult and some translations read it as a phrase rather than a personal name.

name: Perezuzza
dictNote: (breaking of Uzzah), (1 Chronicles 13:11) and PEREZ-UZZAH (2 Samuel 6:8) the title which David conferred on the threshing-floor of Nachon or Cidon, in commemoration of the sudden death of Uzzah. (B.C. 1042.)

name: Tikvah
note: Tikvah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men in the Old Testament carry this name. One was the father of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah, who confirmed the authenticity of the law scroll found during Josiah's temple repairs (2 Kings 22:14). The other was the father of Jahzeiah, one of the few who opposed Ezra's plan to have Israelite men separate from their foreign wives (Ezra 10:15).

name: Ahlai
note: Achlai, the name of an Israelitess and of an Israelite
dictNote: Ahlai is named in 1 Chronicles 2:31 as a child of Sheshan, who according to the surrounding genealogy had no sons, so Ahlai is usually taken to be a daughter through whom the family line continued by way of an Egyptian servant, Jarha. Zabad, one of David's mighty warriors, is called "son of Ahlai" in 1 Chronicles 11:41, likely as a descendant of this same line rather than a direct son.

name: Josias
dictNote: Josias is the Greek form of Josiah, the reforming king of Judah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:10-11). Josiah came to the throne as a boy and later launched a sweeping religious reform after a scroll of the law was discovered during temple repairs, purging idolatrous worship from Judah before his death in battle against Pharaoh Necho.

name: Mezahab
dictNote: Mezahab appears in the Edomite king list of Genesis 36 as the father of Matred and grandfather of Mehetabel, who married Hadar (Hadad), the last king of Edom named in that list (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50).

name: Hammath
dictNote: Warm springs, one of the “fenced cities” of Naphtali (Josh. 19:35). It is identified with the warm baths (the heat of the water ranging from 136 degrees to 144 degrees) still found on the shore a little to the south of Tiberias under the name of Hummam Tabariyeh (“Bath of Tiberias”).

name: Jaaziah
dictNote: Jaaziah was a descendant of Merari, one of the three Levitical clans, listed among those reorganized into divisions of temple service under David (1 Chronicles 24:26-27).

name: Naharai
dictNote: Naharai, from Beeroth, served as armor-bearer to Joab, David's army commander, and is listed among David's mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:37; 1 Chronicles 11:39).

name: Crete
note: a Cretan, i.e. inhabitant of Crete

This man deceived the Jews that were at Crete, and got a great deal of money of them for traveling in splendor; and thence sailed to Melos, where he was thought so certainly genuine, that he got a great deal more money, and prevailed with those that had treated him

dictNote: Crete is the large Mediterranean island where Paul left Titus to organize the churches and appoint elders, and Paul's ship also stopped there during the storm-tossed voyage to Rome recorded in Acts.

name: Jekameam
dictNote: Jekameam was a Levite, one of the sons of Hebron in the Kohathite line, listed among the heads of Levitical divisions organized for temple service under David (1 Chronicles 23:19; 24:23).

name: Nicolaitane
note: a Nicolaite, i.e. adherent of Nicolaus
dictNote: The Nicolaitans were a group active in the churches of Ephesus and Pergamum in the late first century, condemned twice by Christ in the letters of Revelation for teaching or practices linked to idolatry and sexual immorality (Revelation 2:6, 15). Some early church writers connected the name to Nicolas, one of the seven men chosen to serve the Jerusalem church in Acts 6:5, though the link is disputed and little else is known of the group's actual teaching.

name: Eliathah
dictNote: Eliathah was one of the sons of Heman, a Levite musician in David's court, and headed one of the divisions of temple musicians (1 Chronicles 25:4, 27).

name: Bohan
dictNote: Bohan was a Reubenite whose name was given to a boundary stone, "the stone of Bohan," marking part of the border between the territories of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:6; 18:17).

name: Lehabim
note: Lehabim, a son of Mizraim, and his descendants
dictNote: Lehabim appears in the Table of Nations as one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, the biblical ancestor of Egypt (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). The name is widely connected to the Rebu or Lebu people known from Egyptian inscriptions, generally identified as ancestors of the Libyans, who lived along the North African coast west of Egypt.

name: Hezronites
note: a Chetsronite or (collectively) descendants of Chetsron
dictNote: (descendants of Hezron), The.

name: Berothah
note: Berothah or Berothai, a place north of Palestine
dictNote: (toward the wells), Bero’-tha-i (my wells). The first of these two names is given by Ezekiel, (Ezekiel 47:16) in connection with Hahlath and Damascus as forming part of the northern boundary of the promised land. The second is mentioned, (2 Samuel 8:8) in the same connection. The well-known city Beirut (Berytus) naturally suggests itself as identical with one at least of the names; but in each instance the circumstances of the case seem to require a position farther east. They were probably in the vicinity of the springs near the present Hasbeya.

name: Pai
note: Pau or Pai, a place in Edom
dictNote: (blessing). [Pau]

name: Tadmor

secondTemple.excerpt:
When he had therefore built this city, and encompassed it with very strong walls, he gave it the name of Tadmor, and that is the name it is still called by at this day among the Syrians, but the Greeks name it Palmyra.
2.

dictNote: Palm, a city built by Solomon “in the wilderness” (2 Chr. 8:4). In 1 Kings 9:18, where the word occurs in the Authorized Version, the Hebrew text and the Revised Version read “Tamar,” which is properly a city on the southern border of Palestine and toward the wilderness (comp. Ezek. 47:19; 48:28). In 2 Chr. 8:14 Tadmor is mentioned in connection with Hamath-zobah. It is called Palmyra by the Greeks and Romans. It stood in the great Syrian wilderness, 176 miles from Damascus and 130 from the Mediterranean and was the centre of a vast commercial traffic with Western Asia. It was also an important military station. (See SOLOMON.) “Remains of ancient temples and palaces, surrounded by splendid colonnades of white marble, many of which are yet standing, and thousands of prostrate pillars, scattered over a large extent of space, attest the ancient magnificence of this city of palms, surpassing that of the renowned cities of Greece and Rome.”

name: Abimael

secondTemple.excerpt: Now Joctan, one of the sons of Heber, had these sons, Elmodad, Saleph, Asermoth, Jera, Adoram, Aizel, Decla, Ebal, Abimael, Sabeus, Ophir, Euilat, and Jobab.

dictNote: Abimael appears in the Table of Nations as a descendant of Joktan, whose family line is generally located in southern Arabia (Genesis 10:28; 1 Chronicles 1:22).

name: Rumah

secondTemple.excerpt: Now Jehoiakim’s mother was called Zebudah , of the city Rumah.

dictNote: Elevation, probably the same as Arumah (Judg. 9:41; 2 Kings 23:36), near Shechem. Others identify it with Tell Rumeh, in Galilee, about 6 miles north of Nazareth.

name: Tamah
dictNote: Tamah, or Thamah, was the head of a family among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:53; Nehemiah 7:55).

name: Bethshemite
note: a Beth-shimshite, or inhabitant of Bethshemesh

name: Berachah
note: Berakah, the name of an Israelite, and also of a valley in Palestine

secondTemple.excerpt: And on the fourth day, all the people were gathered together, unto a certain hollow place or valley, and blessed God for his power and assistance: from which the place had this name given it, The valley of [Berachah or] blessing .

dictNote: Blessing. (1.) A valley not far from Engedi, where Jehoshaphat overthrew the Moabites and Ammonites (2 Chr. 20:26). It has been identified with the valley of Bereikut. (R.V., “Beracah.”) (2.) One of the Benjamite warriors, Saul’s brethren, who joined David when at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:3).

name: Izrahiah
note: Jizrachjah, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men carry this name. One was a chief of the tribe of Issachar listed in the tribal genealogies (1 Chronicles 7:3). The other was a priest present at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah, generations later (Nehemiah 12:42).

name: Abital
note: Abital, a wife of King David

secondTemple.excerpt: d Arenon; the second was Daniel, by his wife Abigail; the name of the third was Absalom, by Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth he named Adonijah, by his wife Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth he called Ithream, by Eglah.

dictNote: Abital was the fifth of David's wives listed in the record of his family, and the mother of his son Shephatiah, born during David's reign in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:4; 1 Chronicles 3:3).

name: Shomer
note: Shomer, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two people carry this name in the Old Testament. One was the mother of Jehozabad, a royal servant who joined a conspiracy that killed King Joash of Judah; she is called a Moabite and also named Shimrith elsewhere (2 Kings 12:21; 2 Chronicles 24:26). The other was a man of the tribe of Asher, also called Shamer, listed among the heads of his clan (1 Chronicles 7:32, 34).

name: Eltekeh
note: Eltekeh or Elteke, a place in Palestine
dictNote: God is its fear, a city in the tribe of Dan. It was a city of refuge and a Levitical city (Josh. 21:23). It has been identified with Beit-Likia, north-east of latrum.

name: Zimran
note: Zimran, a son of Abraham by Keturah
dictNote: Zimran was a son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, generally taken as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, though the tribe cannot be identified with certainty (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32).

name: Ashur

secondTemple.excerpt: Ashur lived at the city Nineve; and named his subjects Assyrians: who became the most fortunate nation, beyond others.

dictNote: Ashur was a son of Hezron born after his father's death, remembered in Chronicles as the founder of Tekoa (1 Chronicles 2:24; 4:5), the town later home to the prophet Amos.

name: Mathat
note: Matthat (i.e. Mattithjah), the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Luke's genealogy of Jesus lists two different men named Mathat among the ancestors of Joseph, one closer to Joseph's own generation and another, generations further back, near Levi and Melki (Luke 3:24, 29). Little else is recorded about either beyond their place in the genealogical line.

name: Phurah

secondTemple.excerpt: So he obeyed, and went and took his servant Phurah with him.

dictNote: Phurah was Gideon's servant, likely his armor-bearer, who accompanied him on a night reconnaissance of the Midianite camp before Gideon's famous attack with three hundred men (Judges 7:10-11).

name: Hachmoni
dictNote: Hachmoni, or "the Hachmonite," is named as the father of Jehiel, a court official who attended David's sons, and as the family name behind Jashobeam, one of David's chief mighty warriors, whose immediate father was Zabdiel (1 Chronicles 11:11; 27:32).

name: Hephzi-bah
note: Cheptsi-bah, a fanciful name for Palestine
dictNote: Hephzibah, meaning "my delight is in her," was the wife of King Hezekiah of Judah and mother of his son Manasseh (2 Kings 21:1). Isaiah later uses the same name as a symbolic title for restored Jerusalem, picturing the city as once again the object of God's delight rather than an abandoned wife (Isaiah 62:4).

name: Zibiah

secondTemple.excerpt: His mother’s name was Zibiah, of the city Beersheba.

dictNote: Zibiah, from Beersheba, was the mother of King Joash of Judah, the boy king who was hidden from the murderous queen Athaliah and later crowned at age seven (2 Kings 12:1; 2 Chronicles 24:1).

name: Janoah
dictNote: Or Jano’hah, rest. (1.) A town on the north-eastern border of Ephraim, in the Jordan valley (Josh. 16:6, 7). Identified with the modern Yanun, 8 miles south-east of Nablus. (2.) A town of Northern Palestine, within the boundaries of Naphtali. It was taken by the king of Assyria (2 Kings 15:29).

name: Areli
note: Areli (or an Arelite, collectively), an Israelite and his descendants

secondTemple.excerpt: And these are the names of their sons who went with him into Egypt: the sons of Gad: Ziphion, and Haggi, and Shuni, and Ezbon, (and Eri) and Areli, and Arodi--eight.

dictNote: Areli was a son of Gad and ancestor of the Arelite clan, listed among the seventy who went down to Egypt with Jacob and later among the clans counted in the wilderness census (Genesis 46:16; Numbers 26:17).

name: Joshaphat
dictNote: Joshaphat, called "the Mithnite," is listed among David's mighty warriors in the record of his elite fighting men (1 Chronicles 11:43).

name: Immanuel
note: Immanuel, a type name of Isaiah's son
dictNote: Immanuel, meaning "God with us," is not a historical individual but a prophetic name. Isaiah gave it as a sign to King Ahaz, promising that before a child bearing this name grew old enough to know right from wrong, the threat facing Judah would pass (Isaiah 7:14), and used it again as a rallying cry against Judah's enemies (Isaiah 8:8). Matthew's Gospel applies the name to Jesus' birth as its ultimate fulfillment (Matthew 1:23), while the identity of the child originally in view in Isaiah's own day is still debated among interpreters.

name: Adummim
dictNote: Adummim, meaning "the red ones," was a pass on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho, on the boundary between the territories of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:7; 18:17). The rugged, blood-colored rock of the ascent made it a natural setting for banditry, and the location is traditionally associated with the road pictured in Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37).

name: Besai
dictNote: Besai's descendants were among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:49; Nehemiah 7:52).

name: Belteshazzar
note: Belteshatstsar, the Babylonian name of Daniel
dictNote: Belteshazzar was the Babylonian court name given to Daniel by Ashpenaz, the official in charge of the king's court servants, likely honoring the god Bel, following the common Babylonian practice of renaming foreign officials taken into royal service (Daniel 1:3, 7). The name is used throughout the book, including at Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:12) and in Daniel's later visions (Daniel 10:1).

name: Helah
dictNote: Helah was one of two wives of Ashur, the Chronicler's founder of Tekoa, listed in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:5, 7).

name: Shobach

secondTemple.excerpt: ir league, and were liable to be punished for the same, made preparations for war; they also sent a thousand talents to the Syrian king of Mesopotamia, and endeavored to prevail with him to assist them for that pay, and Shobach.

dictNote: Shobach commanded the army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, mustering forces from beyond the Euphrates to fight alongside the Ammonites against David. He was defeated and killed by Joab's forces at Helam, a loss that led the Arameans allied with the Ammonites to make peace with Israel (2 Samuel 10:15-19); he is called Shophach in the parallel account (1 Chronicles 19:16).

name: Luhith
note: Luchith, a place East of the Jordan
dictNote: Made of boards, a Moabitish place between Zoar and Horonaim (Isa. 15:5; Jer. 48:5).

name: Bukkiah
dictNote: Bukkiah was a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman, and headed one of the divisions of temple musicians organized under David (1 Chronicles 25:4, 13).

name: Shiphi
dictNote: Shiphi was a Simeonite, father of Ziza, a leader of his tribe during the reign of Hezekiah, a period when the tribe of Simeon expanded into new pastureland near Gedor (1 Chronicles 4:37-41).

name: Eshbaal
note: Eshbaal (or Ishbosheth), a son of Saul
dictNote: Eshbaal, "man of Baal," was the fourth son of King Saul (1 Chronicles 8:33; 9:39). He is better known by the name Ish-bosheth, "man of shame" (2 Samuel 2:8), a substitution that reflects later Israelite discomfort with the word "Baal" even inside personal names. After Saul's death, Abner made Eshbaal king over the northern tribes for a brief, troubled reign that ended in his assassination, clearing the way for David to rule over a united Israel (2 Samuel 2-4).

name: Buzite
note: a Buzite or descendant of Buz

name: Ishbak

secondTemple.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

dictNote: Ishbak was a son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, traditionally regarded as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, though it cannot be identified with certainty (Genesis 25:2).

name: Kenath
note: Kenath, a place East of the Jordan
dictNote: Possession, a city of Gilead. It was captured by Nobah, who called it by his own name (Num. 32:42). It has been identified with Kunawat, on the slopes of Jebel Hauran (Mount Bashan), 60 miles east from the south end of the Sea of Galilee.

dictNote: Adoram, also called Adoniram, was the official in charge of forced labor under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:6). Years later, King Rehoboam sent him to collect tribute from the northern tribes during the crisis that split the kingdom, and the people stoned him to death, a killing that confirmed the revolt against the house of David (1 Kings 12:18).

name: Ezekias

secondTemple.excerpt: There was also Judas, (16) the son of that Ezekias who had been head of the robbers; which Ezekias was a very strong man, and had with great dificulty been caught by Herod.

(16) Unless this Judas, the son of Ezekias, be the same with that Theudas, mentioned Acts 5:36, Josephus must have omitted him; for that other Thoualas, whom he afterward mentions, under Fadus the Roman governor, B.

dictNote: Ezekias is the Greek form of Hezekiah, used in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:9-10). Hezekiah was a reforming king of Judah who removed idolatrous shrines and survived the Assyrian king Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC, an episode corroborated outside the Bible by Sennacherib's own Prism, which boasts of shutting Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage" but stops short of claiming the city itself was captured.

name: Sacar
note: Sakar, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men carry this name among David's fighting men. One was the father of Ahiam, listed among David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:35). The other was a Korahite gatekeeper of the temple, a son of Obed-edom (1 Chronicles 26:4).

name: Baana
note: Baana, the name of four Israelite

secondTemple.excerpt: of his kindred, and had indeed given him the kingdom, but was greatly afflicted, and Abner's death very much troubled him; nor did he himself outlive any long time, but was treacherously set upon by the sons of Rimmon, (Baanah and Rechab were their names,) and was slain by them; for these being of a family of the Benjamites, and of the first rank among them, thought that if they should slay Ishbosheth, they should obtain large presents from D

dictNote: Three men carry this name. Two were district officers who supplied provisions for Solomon's royal household, one stationed in the region of Megiddo and Taanach (1 Kings 4:12), the other a son of Hushai in a different district (1 Kings 4:16). A third Baana was the father of Zadok, one of those who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:4).

name: Mushites
note: a Mushite (collectively) or descendants of Mushi

name: Ozem
note: Otsem, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men carry this name. One was David's older brother, the sixth of Jesse's sons (1 Chronicles 2:15). The other belonged to a different branch of Judah's genealogy, a son of Jerahmeel (1 Chronicles 2:25).

name: I-chabod
dictNote: Ichabod was born to the wife of Phinehas, Eli's son, just as she was dying in childbirth after hearing that the ark of the covenant had been captured by the Philistines and that both her husband and father-in-law had been killed in the same battle. She named the child Ichabod, meaning "no glory," saying that Israel's glory had departed since the ark was gone (1 Samuel 4:19-22).

name: Cencrea
dictNote: Cenchreae was the eastern harbor town of Corinth, on the Saronic Gulf, roughly seven miles from the city. Paul sailed from there after cutting his hair in fulfillment of a vow (Acts 18:18), and the town had its own church, in which Phoebe served as a deacon and patron whom Paul commends to the Romans (Romans 16:1). Excavations at the site have uncovered its ancient harbor works, confirming its role as one of Corinth's two ports.

name: Shillem
dictNote: Shillem was a son of Naphtali and ancestor of the Shillemite clan, counted among the families of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob and later numbered in the wilderness census; he is also called Shallum in the parallel genealogy of Chronicles (Genesis 46:24; Numbers 26:49; 1 Chronicles 7:13).

name: Alamoth
note: properly, girls, i.e. the soprano or female voice, perhaps falsetto
dictNote: Alamoth is a musical term found in the record of temple worship and in the headings of the Psalms, most likely indicating a high pitch or treble voice, literally "maidens" or "young women" (1 Chronicles 15:20). It appears as the heading of Psalm 46, and probably describes how the psalm was meant to be sung or played rather than naming any person.

name: Zophah
dictNote: Zophah was a son of Helem and a chief of the tribe of Asher, listed at the head of a family record noted for its many able warriors (1 Chronicles 7:35, 40).

name: Gob
dictNote: A pit, a place mentioned in 2 Sam. 21:18, 19; called also Gezer, in 1 Chr. 20:4.

name: Aminadab

secondTemple.excerpt: Of all which Eliab was the eldest: Aminadab the second: Shammah the third: Nathanael the fourth: the fifth was called Rael : and the sixth Asam .

e first day of the second month, of that second year, they set, as overseers of the work, such Levites as were full twenty years old; and Jeshua, and his sons, and brethren, and Cadmiel, the brother of Judas, the son of Aminadab, with his sons.

So when the whole body of the people were come together, as they had resolved to do, the king came to the ark, which the priest brought out of the house of Aminadab, and laid it upon a new cart, and permitted their brethren and their children to draw it, together with the oxen.

dictNote: Aminadab is the Greek form of Amminadab, an ancestor of David through the line of Judah, named in the genealogies of both Matthew and Luke (Matthew 1:4; Luke 3:33). In Exodus, Amminadab's daughter Elisheba married Aaron, linking this family line to Israel's priesthood as well as to its future kings (Exodus 6:23).

name: Aran
dictNote: Aran was a descendant of Seir the Horite, listed among the clan chiefs of Edom in Genesis 36:28 and 1 Chronicles 1:42. The Horites were the indigenous cave-dwelling population of Mount Seir before the Edomites displaced them, and genealogies like this one preserve their tribal structure. Nothing else about him is recorded.

name: Boaz
note: David's great-grandfather, one line in Luke's genealogy (3:32). Josephus retells the whole Book of Ruth as its own episode (spelling the name 'Booz'), explicitly naming the payoff Luke's genealogy is really built toward: the line running straight to David.

secondTemple.excerpt: How under Eli's government of the Israelites, Booz married Ruth: from whom came Obed, the grandfather of David.

dictNote: Alacrity. (1.) The husband of Ruth, a wealthy Bethlehemite. By the “levirate law” the duty devolved on him of marrying Ruth the Moabitess (Ruth 4:1-13). He was a kinsman of Mahlon, her first husband. (2.) The name given (for what reason is unknown) to one of the two (the other was called Jachin) brazen pillars which Solomon erected in the court of the temple (1 Kings 7:21; 2 Chr. 3:17). These pillars were broken up and carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar.

name: Eliud
note: God of majesty; Eliud, an Israelite
dictNote: Eliud appears only in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, listed as the son of Achim and the father of Eleazar, several generations before Joseph (Matthew 1:14-15). Like many names in this section of the genealogy, he is otherwise unknown outside this list. His inclusion reflects Matthew's concern to trace an unbroken line from Abraham to Jesus through the royal house of David.

name: Israelitish
note: a Jisreelitess or female descendant of Jisrael
dictNote: Israelitish is not a personal name but an adjective describing the mother of the man stoned for blasphemy in Leviticus 24:10-11; she is named Shelomith, daughter of Dibri of the tribe of Dan, married to an Egyptian. The passage uses her Israelite identity to raise the legal question of whether the law against blasphemy applied to someone of mixed parentage. God's answer, that one law applies to native and foreigner alike, settles the case.

dictNote: Phares is the Greek form of Perez, listed as an ancestor of Jesus in the genealogies of both Matthew (1:3) and Luke (3:33). dictNote: Two officials named Geber appear among Solomon's twelve district governors responsible for supplying the royal court: “the son of Geber” was stationed at Ramoth-gilead, and Geber son of Uri administered the region of Gilead itself (1 Kings 4:13, 19). Each governor supplied provisions for one month of the year, and Uri's son's territory corresponded to the conquered kingdoms of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan. name: Cushi
note: Cushi, the name of two Israelites

secondTemple.excerpt: He then called Cushi, and committed the business to him, that he should tell the king what he had seen.

dictNote: Cushi, meaning “the Cushite” or “Ethiopian,” is applied to at least two men in the Old Testament: the father of Shelemiah, whose son was sent to summon Baruch after Jeremiah's scroll was burned (Jeremiah 36:14), and an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah (Zephaniah 1:1). The name likely reflects African ancestry or origin somewhere in the family line rather than a single individual, since it recurs at different points in the genealogical record. Some readers connect Zephaniah's own line to royal descent through Hezekiah, named a few generations further back in the same verse.

name: Harsha
dictNote: Harsha, whose name means “worker” or possibly “enchanter,” headed a family of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:52; Nehemiah 7:54). The Nethinim performed menial temple duties and were likely descended from Gibeonites and war captives assigned to that service centuries earlier. Nothing more is recorded of him personally.

dictNote: Huldah was a prophetess in Jerusalem during King Josiah's reign, and when workers repairing the temple discovered a forgotten scroll of the law, Josiah sent his officials directly to Huldah rather than to any of the male prophets active at the time, and she confirmed the scroll's authority and predicted the coming judgment on Judah, though not within Josiah's own lifetime.

name: Hakupha
dictNote: Hakupha's descendants, the Bene-Hakupha, were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel around 538 BC (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). Like most Nethinim family heads, nothing is known of Hakupha beyond this listing. The parallel lists in Ezra and Nehemiah preserve slightly different numbers for the returning families, reflecting the difficulty of transmitting census figures across generations of copying.

name: Migron

dictNote: Jechonias is the Greek form of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, the young king of Judah exiled to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar after a three-month reign (2 Kings 24:8-15); Matthew's genealogy lists him at the pivotal generation marking the exile (Matthew 1:11-12). Babylonian ration tablets excavated in the city and dated to Nebuchadnezzar's reign list regular food allotments for “Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud” and his sons, confirming that the exiled king was kept alive and provided for at the Babylonian court, exactly as 2 Kings 25:27-30 describes decades later. Jeremiah had pronounced a curse that none of his descendants would sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30), a tension Matthew resolves by tracing Jesus' legal, not biological, throne-right through Joseph rather than a reigning bloodline.

name: Aliah
dictNote: Aliah is an alternate spelling of Alvah, one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Esau (Genesis 36:40; 1 Chronicles 1:51). The two Edomite king-lists in Genesis and Chronicles show minor spelling variation of this kind throughout. Nothing further is recorded of him.

dictNote: This entry actually concerns the Aramaic title “Rabboni,” used twice in the Gospels to address Jesus directly: by the blind beggar Bartimaeus at Jericho (Mark 10:51) and by Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb (John 20:16). It is an intensified, more reverential form of “Rabbi,” closer to “my great master” or “my lord and teacher.” Both speakers use it in moments of urgent personal appeal to Jesus rather than as a formal title.

name: Uzzielites
note: an Uzzielite (collectively) or descendants of Uzziel

name: Jahzeel
dictNote: Jahzeel was the first of Naphtali's four sons who went to Egypt with Jacob's household (Genesis 46:24), and he became ancestor of the Jahzeelite clan counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:48). Nothing else is recorded of him.

name: Mahaneh-dan
dictNote: Judg. 18:12 = “camp of Dan” 13:25 (R.V., “Mahaneh-dan”), a place behind (i.e., west of) Kirjath-jearim, where the six hundred Danites from Zorah and Eshtaol encamped on their way to capture the city of Laish, which they rebuilt and called “Dan, after the name of their father” (18:11-31). The Palestine Explorers point to a ruin called ‘Erma, situated about 3 miles from the great corn valley on the east of Samson’s home.

name: Rahab

(2) It plainly appears by the history of these spies, and the innkeeper Rahab’s deception of the King of Jericho’s messengers, by telling them what was false, in order to save the lives of the spies, and yet the great commendation of her faith and good works in the New Testament, Heb.

dictNote: This Greek form “Rhaab” refers to Rahab, the Canaanite woman of Jericho who hid Israel's spies and was spared when the city fell (Joshua 2, 6). The New Testament cites her twice as an example of faith expressed through action: Hebrews 11:31 credits her rescue to faith, and James 2:25 points to her sheltering of the spies as proof that faith without works is dead. She later married Salmon and became an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), one of only a few women named in that genealogy.

name: Beth-gilgal
dictNote: House of Gilgal, a place from which the inhabitants gathered for the purpose of celebrating the rebuilding of the walls on the return exile (Neh. 12:29). (See GILGAL.)

name: Rissah
note: Rissah, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Heap of ruins; dew, a station of the Israelites in the wilderness (Num. 33:21, 22).

name: Bakbuk
dictNote: Bakbuk's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). The name means “bottle” or “flask,” possibly an occupational designation from an ancestor's trade. Nothing more is known of him.

name: Shuah

secondTemple.excerpt: And she bare him six sons, Zimram, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah, in the two weeks of years.

dictNote: Two men named Shuah appear in genealogies: one was a son Abraham had by his second wife Keturah, whose descendants settled in Arabia and gave their name to the “Shuhites,” the people of Job's friend Bildad (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32); the other is a much briefer mention in the tribe of Judah's genealogy as father of Chelub (1 Chronicles 4:11). The two are unrelated apart from sharing a name.

name: Nergal-sharezer
note: Nergal-Sharetser, the name of two Babylonians
dictNote: Nergal-sharezer, named for the Babylonian god Nergal, appears among the officials of Nebuchadnezzar's army at the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and one bearing the additional title “Rab-mag” helped release Jeremiah from prison (Jeremiah 39:3, 13). Scholars generally identify this official with Neriglissar, the Babylonian general who later murdered his brother-in-law Evil-Merodach (Amel-Marduk) and reigned as king from about 560 to 556 BC. Neriglissar's short reign and violent seizure of the throne are independently confirmed by Babylonian chronicles and king lists.

name: Eliam
dictNote: Eliam appears in two contexts that may describe the same man: as the father of Bathsheba, David's wife (2 Samuel 11:3, where Chronicles gives his name as Ammiel), and as the son of David's counselor Ahithophel and one of David's elite thirty warriors (2 Samuel 23:34). If the two references are the same person, it would mean Bathsheba was Ahithophel's granddaughter, which some read as a motive behind Ahithophel's bitter betrayal of David during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 15-17).

name: Charran
note: Charrhan (i.e. Charan), a place in Mesopotamia

dictNote: Another form (Acts 7:2, 4) of Haran (q.v.).

name: Magdiel
dictNote: Magdiel was one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Esau, listed in the Edomite king-and-chief records of Genesis 36:43 and 1 Chronicles 1:54. Nothing else is recorded of him individually; his name marks a clan territory rather than necessarily one ruler.

name: Bilshan
dictNote: Bilshan was one of the leaders who returned to Judah from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel around 538 BC (Ezra 2:2; Nehemiah 7:7). His name, meaning roughly “eloquent” or “man of the tongue,” suggests he may have served as a spokesman for the returning community, though nothing further is recorded of his role.

name: Gazzam
dictNote: Gazzam's descendants, the Bene-Gazzam, were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:48; Nehemiah 7:51). Nothing further is known of him.

name: Peleth
note: Peleth, the name of two Israelites

secondTemple.excerpt: But if God had determined to bestow it on the eldest tribe; that of Reubel might have it most justly: and then Dathan, and Abiram, and [On the son of] Peleth would have it.

dictNote: Two men named Peleth appear in the Old Testament: a Reubenite whose son On joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Numbers 16:1), and a son of Jonathan in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:33). The two belong to different tribes and different eras and are otherwise unrelated.

name: Hazarmaveth
dictNote: (court of death), the third in order of the sons of Joktan (Genesis 10:26) The name is preserved in the Arabic Hadramawt and Hadrumawl, the appellation of a province and an ancient people of southern Arabia. The capital is Satham, a very ancient city, and its chief ports are Mirbat, Zafari and Kisheem, from whence a great trade was carried on in ancient times with India and Africa.

name: Gilonite
note: a Gilonite or inhabitant of Giloh

secondTemple.excerpt: Among them came Ahithophel the Gilonite, a counsellor of David's, and two hundred men out of Jerusalem itself, who knew not his intentions, but were sent for as to a sacrifice.

name: Shobai
dictNote: Shobai's descendants, gatekeepers of the temple, were among those who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:42; Nehemiah 7:45). His name means “captor” or “captive.” Nothing further is recorded of him.

name: Adonizedec
dictNote: Adonizedec was the Amorite king of Jerusalem who organized a coalition of five Canaanite kings to attack Gibeon after it made peace with Israel, prompting Joshua's forces to march to Gibeon's defense in the battle where the sun and moon reportedly stood still (Joshua 10:1-13). His coalition was defeated and the five kings were captured, humiliated, and executed (Joshua 10:16-27). His name, meaning “lord of righteousness,” echoes the earlier Melchizedek, priest-king of the same city centuries before (Genesis 14:18), and the fourteenth-century BC Amarna letters independently show Jerusalem ruled by its own king corresponding with Egypt around this period, confirming the city's status as an established Canaanite city-state.

name: Adbeel
dictNote: Adbeel was the third of Ishmael's twelve sons, each of whom became head of an Arabian tribal confederation (Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29). Some scholars connect his descendants with the “Idibi'ilu” named in the eighth-century BC annals of the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III as a tribe controlling Egypt's desert border. Nothing further is recorded of Adbeel himself.

name: Bene-jaakan
note: Bene-Jaakan, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Children of Jaakan (Num. 33:31, 32), the same as Beeroth.

name: Mahlites
note: a Machlite or (collectively) descendants of Machli

name: Evi

dictNote: Evi was one of five Midianite kings, described elsewhere as princes vassal to the Amorite king Sihon, killed by Israel's forces in the war of vengeance against Midian (Numbers 31:8), and his territory is recalled among the lands allotted afterward (Joshua 13:21). The campaign was ordered in response to Midian's role in luring Israel into idolatry and immorality at Baal-peor (Numbers 25; 31:1-2). Nothing more is known of Evi individually.

name: Mithcah
note: Mithkah, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Sweetness, one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (Num. 33:28, 29).

name: Rezeph
dictNote: Solid; a stone, (2 Kings 19:12; Isa. 37:12), a fortress near Haran, probably on the west of the Euphrates, conquered by Sennacherib.

name: Eltolad
dictNote: (God’s kindred), one of the cities in the south of Judah, (Joshua 15:30) allotted to Simeon, (Joshua 19:4) and in possession of that tribe until the time of David. (1 Chronicles 4:29)

name: Medad
dictNote: Medad was one of seventy elders appointed to share the burden of leading Israel with Moses; when the Spirit came upon the group, he and his companion Eldad prophesied in the camp rather than at the tent of meeting with the others (Numbers 11:26-27). Joshua wanted Moses to stop them, but Moses answered that he wished all the Lord's people were prophets (Numbers 11:28-29). Nothing else is recorded of him.

name: Sheva

secondTemple.excerpt: He made Sheva the scribe, and appointed Zadok and Abiathar the high priests.

dictNote: Two men named Sheva appear in the Old Testament: a son of Caleb in the tribal genealogy of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:49), and one of David's royal scribes or secretaries (2 Samuel 20:25), likely the same official called Seraiah or Shisha elsewhere in the parallel lists of David's officials. Nothing more is recorded of either.

name: Pathrusim

name: Calah
dictNote: One of the most ancient cities of Assyria. “Out of that land he [i.e., Nimrod] went forth into Assyria, and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah, and Resen” (Gen. 10:11, R.V.). Its site is now marked probably by the Nimrud ruins on the left bank of the Tigris. These cover an area of about 1,000 acres, and are second only in size and importance to the mass of ruins opposite Mosul. This city was at one time the capital of the empire, and was the residence of Sardanapalus and his successors down to the time of Sargon, who built a new capital, the modern Khorsabad. It has been conjectured that these four cities mentioned in Gen. 10:11 were afterwards all united into one and called Nineveh (q.v.).

name: Chisleu
dictNote: Chisleu, also spelled Kislev, is not a person but the name of the ninth month of the Hebrew religious calendar, roughly corresponding to late November and December, adopted from the Babylonians after the exile (Nehemiah 1:1; Zechariah 7:1). It marks the season in which Nehemiah heard the report of Jerusalem's broken walls and Zechariah received several of his visions. The later festival of Hanukkah also falls in this month, though it is not mentioned in these particular passages.

name: Hezir
note: Chezir, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Hezir appear in the postexilic records: the head of the seventeenth division of priests organized by David for temple service (1 Chronicles 24:15), and a leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant of reform after the exile (Nehemiah 10:20). Whether the two are related is not stated. A first-century BC tomb in Jerusalem's Kidron Valley, known as the Tomb of the Sons of Hezir, bears an inscription naming a priestly family by this name, showing it remained in use among Jerusalem's priesthood for centuries.

name: Thebez
dictNote: Brightness, a place some 11 miles north-east of Shechem, on the road to Scythopolis, the modern Tabas. Abimelech led his army against this place, because of its participation in the conspiracy of the men of Shechem; but as he drew near to the strong tower to which its inhabitants had fled for safety, and was about to set fire to it, a woman cast a fragment of millstone at him, and “all to brake his skull” i.e., “altogether brake,” etc. His armourbearer thereupon “thrust him through, and he died” (Judg. 9:50-55).

name: Meronothite
note: a Meronothite, or inhabitant of some (otherwise unknown) Meronoth.
dictNote: A name given to Jehdeiah, the herdsman of the royal asses in the time of David and Solomon (1 Chr. 27:30), probably as one being a native of some unknown town called Meronoth.

name: Pisidia
note: Pisidia, a region of Asia Minor
dictNote: A district in Asia Minor, to the north of Pamphylia. The Taurus range of mountains extends through it. Antioch, one of its chief cities, was twice visited by Paul (Acts 13:14; 14:21-24).

placePhoto.description: panorama of a mountain and ancient theater at Termessos in Pisidia

name: Massa
dictNote: Massa was one of Ishmael's twelve sons, each the head of an Arabian tribal confederation (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). Assyrian records from the eighth century BC mention a nomadic Arabian tribe called “Mas'a” in the same general region, which many scholars identify with his descendants. Nothing further is recorded of Massa himself.

name: Beth-dagon
note: Beth-Dagon, the name of two places in Palestine
dictNote: Beth-dagon, meaning “house of Dagon,” names two separate towns rather than a person: one in the lowland plain of Judah near Philistine territory (Joshua 15:41), identified with modern Beit Dajan near Lydda, and another on the southeastern border of Asher (Joshua 19:27). Both names preserve the memory of shrines to Dagon, the chief god of the Philistines, whose worship is also recorded at Ashdod in the account of the captured ark of the covenant (1 Samuel 5:1-5).

name: Helek
dictNote: Helek was a descendant of Manasseh through Gilead, head of the Helekite clan counted in the wilderness census and later allotted land in Gilead (Numbers 26:30; Joshua 17:2). Nothing further is recorded of him individually.

name: Zereda
dictNote: The fortress, a city on the north of Mount Ephraim; the birthplace of Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:26). It is probably the same as Zaretan (Josh. 3:16), Zererath (Judg. 7:22), Zartanah (1 Kings 4:12), or the following.

name: Zif
dictNote: Zif is not a person but the name of the second month of the ancient Hebrew calendar, meaning “brightness” or “blossoming,” later called Iyar; it is used only to date the start of Solomon's temple construction, in the fourth year of his reign, and its completion seven years later (1 Kings 6:1, 37). The month falls roughly in April and May.

name: Irijah
dictNote: Irijah was a captain of the guard at Jerusalem's Benjamin Gate who arrested the prophet Jeremiah as he tried to leave the city during a lull in the Babylonian siege, accusing him of deserting to the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 37:13-14). He handed Jeremiah over to the princes, who had him beaten and imprisoned. Jeremiah maintained his innocence, but the episode led to a long and dangerous confinement (Jeremiah 37:15-21).

name: Eldaah
dictNote: Eldaah was the youngest of Midian's sons and grandson of Abraham through Keturah, becoming ancestor of one of the Arabian tribal groups descended from Midian (Genesis 25:4; 1 Chronicles 1:33). Nothing further is recorded of him.

name: Harhur
dictNote: Harhur's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:51; Nehemiah 7:53). His name means “fever” or possibly “inflammation.” Nothing more is known of him.

name: Agabus

secondTemple.excerpt: Hudson’s Note here: “This, says he, is that famine foretold by Agabus Acts 11:28.

dictNote: Agabus was a Christian prophet in the early church who, at Antioch, predicted a severe famine that later occurred during the reign of Claudius, prompting the church to send relief to believers in Judea (Acts 11:27-30). Years later he met Paul at Caesarea and dramatically bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to warn that Paul would be arrested and handed over to the Gentiles if he went to Jerusalem, a warning Paul heeded as a caution but not a command to turn back (Acts 21:10-14). His famine prediction is one of the clearer instances in Acts of a specific, later-verified prophecy.

name: Imri
note: Imri, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Imri appear in postexilic records: an ancestor of a family from the tribe of Judah listed among those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:4), and the father of Zaccur, who helped rebuild a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 3:2). Whether they are the same person is not stated.

name: Zaavan
dictNote: Zaavan, also called Zavan, was one of the tribal chiefs (“dukes”) of Edom descended from Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:27; 1 Chronicles 1:42). Nothing further is recorded of him.

name: Mattathias
note: Mattathias (i.e. Mattithjah), an Israelite and a Christian

Only we may note, by the way, that the original name of these Maccabees, and their posterity, was Asamoneans; which was derived from Asamoneus, the great-grandfather of Mattathias, as Josephus here informs us.

id lest they should be caught in the midst between two bodies, and perish; so they ran away in haste, and indeed all the rest left Jonathan; but a few there were, in number about fifty, who staid with him, and with them Mattathias, the son of Absalom, and Judas, the son of Chapseus, who were commanders of the whole army.

dictNote: Two men named Mattathias appear consecutively in Luke's genealogy of Jesus: the son of Amos and the son of Semein, both several generations before Joseph (Luke 3:25-26). Neither is otherwise known; the name, meaning “gift of the Lord,” was common enough to later be borne by the priest who launched the Maccabean revolt roughly a century and a half before Jesus, though that Mattathias is a different, unrelated figure.

name: Tel-haresha
dictNote: Hill of the wood, a place in Babylon from which some captive Jews returned to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:59; Neh. 7:61).

name: Shophach
dictNote: Shophach, also spelled Shobach in the parallel account, was the general commanding the army of Hadadezer, the Aramean king of Zobah, when Ammon hired Aramean mercenaries against David; Joab's forces defeated the coalition and killed Shophach in battle (1 Chronicles 19:16-18; compare 2 Samuel 10:16-18). His death broke Aramean support for Ammon and led several vassal kings to make peace with David. The battle marks the high point of David's wars establishing Israelite dominance over the Aramean states to the north.

name: Tabaoth
dictNote: Tabaoth's descendants were among the families of temple servants (Nethinim) who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43; Nehemiah 7:46). Nothing further is recorded of him.

name: Pelet
note: Pelet, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Two men named Pelet appear in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles: a descendant of Judah through Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47), and a Benjamite warrior, skilled with bow and sling, who joined David's growing band of fighters at Ziklag while he was still fleeing Saul (1 Chronicles 12:2-3). The two belong to different tribes and are unrelated.

name: Appaim
dictNote: Appaim was a son of Nadab in the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah's tribe, one of the family lines that helped establish Judah's prominence among the twelve tribes (1 Chronicles 2:30-31). His own line continued through his son Ishi. Nothing further is recorded of him.

name: Tidal

secondTemple.excerpt: twelve years; and so long they continued to pay their tribute: but on the thirteenth year they rebelled; and then the army of the Assyrians came upon them, under their commanders, Amraphel , Arioch , Chodorlaomor , and Tidal .

dictNote: Tidal, called “king of nations” (Hebrew “Goyim”), was one of four eastern kings, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, who campaigned against a coalition of Canaanite cities and carried off Lot before Abraham pursued and defeated them (Genesis 14:1-16). His name corresponds to Tudhaliya, a royal name borne by several Hittite kings, and “Goyim” most likely designates a confederation of peoples east of the Tigris rather than a single nation. The episode is the Bible's earliest recorded military campaign and treats Abraham as a regional power capable of defeating an organized royal coalition.

name: Michaiah
note: Mikajah, the name of an Israelite and an Israelitess

secondTemple.excerpt: He left behind him twenty-two sons, and sixteen daughters; and he had also those children by fourteen wives; and Asa his son succeeded in the kingdom; and the young man's mother was Michaiah.

dictNote: The name Michaiah is applied to several distinct people in the Old Testament: the mother of King Abijah of Judah, likely the same woman elsewhere called Maacah (2 Chronicles 13:2); one of the officials Jehoshaphat sent throughout Judah to teach the law (2 Chronicles 17:7); a man present when the high priest Hilkiah reported discovery of the law book to King Josiah's officials (2 Kings 22:12); the son of Gemariah, who reported Jeremiah's warnings to the royal court after hearing Baruch read the scroll aloud (Jeremiah 36:11-13); and a Levite and a priest, both involved in the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:35, 41). The recurrence of the name across these different roles and generations shows it was common rather than tied to one notable figure.

name: Paltiel
note: Paltiel, the name of two Israelites

secondTemple.excerpt: So Abner took Michal from Phaltiel, who was then her husband, and sent her to David, Ishbosheth himself affording him his assistance, for David had written to him that of right he ought to have this his wife restored to him.

dictNote: Two men named Paltiel appear in the Old Testament: the prince of the tribe of Issachar appointed to help divide the promised land among the tribes (Numbers 34:26), and Paltiel son of Laish, to whom King Saul gave his daughter Michal after taking her from David; when Abner later returned Michal to David, Paltiel followed her weeping until Abner ordered him home (2 Samuel 3:15-16). The two references belong to entirely different periods and are unrelated apart from the shared name, also written “Palti” in 1 Samuel 25:44.

name: Messias
dictNote: Messias is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew and Aramaic “Messiah,” meaning “anointed one,” used only twice in the New Testament: by Andrew telling his brother Simon Peter that he had found the Messiah (John 1:41), and by the Samaritan woman at the well telling Jesus she knew Messiah was coming (John 4:25). John immediately glosses the term for his Greek-speaking readers as “the Christ,” since “Christos” is the Greek equivalent. Both scenes mark the term's first appearance on the lips of ordinary people recognizing Jesus rather than in prophetic or narrative description.

name: Lo-ammi
note: Lo-Ammi, the symbolic name of a son of Hosea
dictNote: Lo-ammi, meaning “not my people,” was the symbolic name God commanded the prophet Hosea to give his second son by Gomer, representing God's coming rejection of the northern kingdom of Israel for its unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:9). The name is deliberately reversed later in the book, where God promises that those once called “not my people” will be called “sons of the living God” (Hosea 1:10; 2:23), a reversal Paul later applies to the inclusion of Gentiles among God's people (Romans 9:25-26). Hosea's children's names function as a set of acted prophecies rather than ordinary personal names.

name: Tirhakah
dictNote: Tirhakah, known in Egyptian and Kushite records as Taharqa, ruled Egypt and Kush as pharaoh of the twenty-fifth (Kushite) dynasty in the early seventh century BC. The Bible names him as the Kushite king whose advance against Assyria prompted Sennacherib to send a threatening message to Hezekiah during the siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:9; Isaiah 37:9). Assyrian records confirm his historicity in detail: the annals and inscribed prisms of both Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal describe their invasions of Egypt and repeated defeats of Taharqa, who was eventually driven back into Nubia.

name: Rogelim
note: Rogelim, a place East of the Jordan
dictNote: Fullers, a town of Gilead, the residence of Barzillai the Gileadite (2 Sam. 17:27; 19:31), probably near to Mahanaim.

name: Matred
dictNote: Matred was the daughter of Mezahab and mother of Mehetabel, who married Hadar (also called Hadad), the last king of Edom named in the Genesis king-list before Israel's own kings arose (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50). She is one of the few women named in these otherwise male genealogical lists. Nothing further is recorded of her.

name: Mahazioth
dictNote: Mahazioth was a Kohathite Levite, one of the sons of Heman appointed by David to lead temple music, and he headed the twenty-third of the twenty-four courses of musicians who served on a rotating schedule (1 Chronicles 25:4, 30-31). His name means “visions,” fitting a family whose musical service was described as prophesying with instruments (1 Chronicles 25:1). Nothing else is recorded of him.

name: Palti
note: Palti, the name of two Israelites

secondTemple.excerpt: 17 For as to Michal, the daughter of King Saul, who had been David’s wife, her father had given her in marriage to Phalti, the son of Laish, who was of the city of Gallim.

dictNote: Palti was one of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan, representing the tribe of Benjamin (Numbers 13:9). A different man named Palti, son of Laish, was the husband Saul gave Michal after David fled the court; when David later reclaimed her as his wife, Palti followed her weeping until Abner ordered him back home (1 Samuel 25:44; 2 Samuel 3:14-16).

name: Baladan
note: Baladan, the name of a Babylonian prince

secondTemple.excerpt: 709.] At this time it was that the dominion of the Assyrians was overthrown by the Medes.  But of these things I shall treat elsewhere.1 But the King of Babylon, whose name was Baladan, sent ambassadors to Hezekiah, with presents; and desired he would be his ally, and his friend.

dictNote: Baladan appears only as the father of Merodach-baladan, the Babylonian king who sent envoys to Hezekiah after his illness (2 Kings 20:12; Isaiah 39:1). Nothing else about him is recorded in the biblical text; his son's rebellions against Assyria are independently attested in Assyrian and Babylonian chronicle records of the period.

name: Hillel

secondTemple.excerpt: 1178] Abdon also, the son of Hillel, of the tribe of Ephraim, and born at the city Pyrathon, was ordained their supreme governor after Helon.

dictNote: Hillel was a Pirathonite from the hill country of Ephraim, the father of Abdon, one of the minor judges who governed Israel after Jephthah (Judges 12:13, 15). Nothing more is recorded about him, and he is not related to the later rabbinic sage of the same name who taught in Jerusalem centuries afterward.

name: Mered
dictNote: Mered was a descendant of Judah through the line of Ezra, listed among the tribe's families in the genealogies of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 4:17-18). He is recorded as having married Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh, alongside a wife from the Judahite line called "the Jewess," and various towns and craftsmen were reckoned among his descendants.

name: Casluhim
note: Casluchim, a people cognate to the Egyptians
dictNote: Casluhim was not an individual but one of the peoples descended from Mizraim, the biblical ancestor of Egypt, in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13-14; 1 Chronicles 1:11-12). Genesis names the Philistines as coming from this group, placing their origin somewhere along the eastern Nile delta or the Mediterranean coast near Egypt's border with Canaan.

name: Arvad
dictNote: Wandering, (Ezek. 27:8), a small island and city on the coast of Syria, mentioned as furnishing mariners and soldiers for Tyre. The inhabitants were called Arvadites. The name is written Aruada or Arada in the Tell-el-Amarna tablets.

name: Madon
dictNote: Strife, a Canaanitish city in the north of Palestine (Josh. 11:1; 12:19), whose king was slain by Joshua; perhaps the ruin Madin, near Hattin, some 5 miles west of Tiberias.

name: Cheran
dictNote: Cheran was one of the sons of Dishon, a Horite chief listed among the clans of Seir before Edom's kings arose (Genesis 36:26; 1 Chronicles 1:41). The Horites were the region's earlier inhabitants, later displaced or absorbed by Esau's descendants.

name: Merom
dictNote: Merom was not a person but the waters, likely the marshy lake north of the Sea of Galilee now called Lake Huleh, where Joshua won his climactic victory over the northern Canaanite coalition led by Jabin, king of Hazor (Joshua 11:5-7). Hazor's massive Late Bronze Age destruction layer, one of the best documented in Canaanite archaeology, corresponds to this period, even though the mound itself lies a few miles from the waters.

name: Elzabad
note: Elzabad, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Elzabad was the name of two different men in Chronicles. One was a Gadite warrior who joined David's band at Ziklag before he became king (1 Chronicles 12:8-13), and the other was a son of Shemaiah, a Korahite Levite serving as a gatekeeper of the temple (1 Chronicles 26:7).

name: Bithynia

secondTemple.excerpt: Now Antonius and Caesar had beaten Cassius near Philippi, as others have related; but after the victory, Caesar went into Gaul, [Italy,] and Antony marched for Asia, who, when he was arrived at Bithynia, he had ambassadors that met him from all parts.

But when Caesar and Antony had slain Cassius near Philippi, and Caesar was gone to Italy, and Antony to Asia, amongst the rest of the cities which sent ambassadors to Antony unto Bithynia, the great men of the Jews came also, and accused Phasaelus and Herod, that they kept the government by force, and that Hyrcanus had no more than an honorable name.

How strong a plea may Bithynia, and Cappadocia, and the people of Pamphylia, the Lycians, and Cilicians, put in for liberty! But they are made tributary without an army.

ering districts of Egypt, Phoenicia, Syria in general, and especially that part of it which is called Coelo-Syria, and also with those more distant regions of Pamphylia, Cilicia, the greater part of Asia Minor as far as Bithynia, and the furthermost corners of Pontus.

dictNote: A province in Asia Minor, to the south of the Euxine and Propontis. Christian congregations were here formed at an early time (1 Pet. 1:1). Paul was prevented by the Spirit from entering this province (Acts 16:7). It is noted in church history as the province ruled over by Pliny as Roman proconsul, who was perplexed as to the course he should take with the numerous Christians brought before his tribunal on account of their profession of Christianity and their conduct, and wrote to Trajan, the emperor, for instructions (A.D. 107).

name: Zemaraim

secondTemple.excerpt: , he was not affrighted at it, but proved of a courageous temper of mind, superior both to his youth and to the hopes of his enemy; so he chose him an army out of the two tribes, and met Jeroboam at a place called Mount Zemaraim, and pitched his camp near the other, and prepared everything necessary for the fight.

dictNote: (1.) A town of Benjamin (Josh. 18:22); now the ruin, rather two ruins, es-Sumrah, 4 miles north of Jericho. (2.) A mount in the highlands of Ephraim, to the north of Jerusalem (2 Chr. 13:4-20). Here the armies of Abijah and Jeroboam engaged in a bloody battle, which issued in the total defeat of the king of Israel, who never “recovered strength again,” and soon after died.

name: Jaala
note: Jaala or Jaalah, one of the Nethinim
dictNote: Jaala headed a family among the Nethinim, the temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:56; Nehemiah 7:58). The Nethinim performed menial temple duties and are traditionally traced back to Gibeonites and war captives assigned to Levitical service.

name: Shaaph
note: Shaaph, the name of two Israelites
dictNote: Shaaph was the name of two men in Caleb's genealogy in Chronicles. One was a son of Jahdai (1 Chronicles 2:47), and the other was a son Caleb had by his concubine Maacah, remembered as the founder or ruler of the town of Madmannah (1 Chronicles 2:49).

name: Joanna
dictNote: Joanna was the name of two figures connected to Luke's Gospel. One was an ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, apparently the same man Chronicles calls Hananiah, a descendant of Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27; 1 Chronicles 3:19). The other Joanna was the wife of Chuza, a steward of Herod Antipas; she helped support Jesus' ministry financially, and she was among the women who found the empty tomb and reported it to the apostles (Luke 8:3; 24:10).

name: Meah
dictNote: Meah, meaning "the hundred," was not a person but a tower on Jerusalem's northern wall, rebuilt by the priests as part of Nehemiah's post-exilic restoration of the city's defenses (Nehemiah 3:1; 12:39). Its name most likely marked either its height in cubits or a measurement tied to the surrounding wall section.

name: Haradah
note: Charadah, a place in the Desert
dictNote: Fright; fear, the twenty-fifth station of the Israelites in their wanderings (Num. 33:24).

name: Shamma
dictNote: Shamma was a son of Zophar, listed among the leading men of the tribe of Asher in Israel's genealogies (1 Chronicles 7:37). He is distinct from Shammah, son of Agee, one of David's three mightiest warriors; the two names are spelled differently in Hebrew despite their similar English rendering.

name: Rufus

dictNote: Rufus was the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man compelled to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha; Mark names him alongside his brother Alexander as someone his original readers would recognize (Mark 15:21). Paul later greets a Rufus in Rome and calls his mother a mother to him as well, which many take to be the same family, since Mark's Gospel is traditionally linked to the Roman church (Romans 16:13).

name: Minnith
note: Minnith, a place East of the Jordan

secondTemple.excerpt: home in safety, to offer in sacrifice what living creature soever should first meet him, he joined battel with the enemy; and gained a great victory; and in his pursuit slew the enemies all along, as far as the city of Minnith.

dictNote: Distribution, an Ammonitish town (Judg. 11:33) from which wheat was exported to Tyre (Ezek. 27:17). It was probably somewhere in the Mishor or table-land on the east of Jordan. There is a gentle valley running for about 4 miles east of Dhiban called Kurm Dhiban, “the vineyards of Dibon.” Tristram supposes that this may be the “vineyards” mentioned in Judg. (l.c.).

name: Enaim
note: Enajim or Enam, a place in Palestine

secondTemple.excerpt:
Testament of Judah, Chapter 12

name: Diklah
dictNote: (palm grove). (Genesis 10:27; 1 Chronicles 1:21) a son of Joktan, whose settlements, in common with those of the other sons of Joktan, must be looked for in Arabia. It is thought that Diklah is a part of Arabia containing many palm trees.

name: Neziah
dictNote: Neziah headed a family of Nethinim, temple servants whose descendants returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:54; Nehemiah 7:56). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Sotai
dictNote: Sotai headed a family descended from "Solomon's servants," a class of temple workers grouped alongside the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:55; Nehemiah 7:57). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Jochebed

secondTemple.excerpt: For it is not to be supposed that the Author of these institutions is barely Moses, the son of Amram, and Jochebed; but he who obliged the Nile to run bloody for your sakes; and tamed the haughtiness of the Egyptians by various sorts of judgments: he who provided a way through the sea for us: he who contrived a method of sending us
When the vision had informed him of these things, Amram awaked and told it to Jochebed who was his wife.
And she went and called thy mother Jochebed,  and she gave her wages, and she nursed thee.
And Jochebed was born in Egypt, in my sixty-fourth year, for I was renowned then in the midst of my brethren.
And in the ninety-fourth year Ambram took Jochebed my daughter to him to wife, for they were born in one 5 day, he and my daughter.

dictNote: Jochebed was the wife of Amram and the mother of Miriam, Aaron, and Moses (Numbers 26:59). She hid the infant Moses for three months and then placed him in a basket on the Nile to save him from Pharaoh's decree, and later nursed him as his hired wet nurse after Pharaoh's daughter drew him from the water (Exodus 2:1-10).

name: Ribai
dictNote: Ribai was a Benjamite from Gibeah, the father of Ittai, one of David's thirty mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:29; 1 Chronicles 11:31). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Arbahite
note: an Arbathite or inhabitant of (Beth-) Arabah

name: Tabeal
note: Tabeel, the name of a Syrian and of a Persian
dictNote: Tabeal, also spelled Tabeel, is used of two different men. One was the father of a man whom the kings of Syria and Israel plotted to install on Judah's throne in place of Ahaz, a scheme Isaiah confronted with his sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:1-6). The other was a Persian-appointed official in Samaria who joined in writing a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:7-8).

name: Cherith
dictNote: Cherith was not a person but a ravine with a seasonal stream where the prophet Elijah hid and was fed by ravens during the early part of a three-year drought under King Ahab (1 Kings 17:2-6). Its exact location is uncertain; proposals range from the Wadi Qelt near Jericho to ravines further east in Gilead.

Hereupon he left one whose name was Lysias, who was in great repute with him governor of the kingdom, as far as the bounds of Egypt, and of the Lower Asia, and reaching from the river Euphrates, and committed to him a certain part of his forces, and of his eleph
