name: Diblaim
dictNote: Diblaim was the father of Gomer, the woman the prophet Hosea married at God's command as a living symbol of Israel's unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:3). Nothing further is known of Diblaim.

name: Abdiel
dictNote: Abdiel was a Gadite chief listed in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 5:15. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Jekabzeel
dictNote: (what God gathers), a fuller form of the name of Kabzeel, the most remote city of Judah on the southern frontier. (Nehemiah 11:25)

name: Adalia
dictNote: Adalia was one of the ten sons of Haman who were killed by the Jews of Susa in self-defense on the day set for their destruction, and whose bodies were afterward hanged (Esther 9:7-10).

name: Chileab
dictNote: Chileab was David's second son, born to Abigail after David married her following the death of her first husband Nabal (2 Samuel 3:3). He is called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1. He is never mentioned again after his birth notice and is generally thought to have died young, since he plays no role in the succession disputes among David's other sons.

name: Fortunatus

secondTemple.excerpt: 22 And as soon as he heard they set sail, he sent Fortunatus, one of his freed men, to Rome; to carry presents to the Emperor, and letters against Herod; and to give Caius a particular account of those matters, if he should have any opportunity.

dictNote: Fortunatus was a Christian of Corinth who, with Stephanas and Achaicus, traveled to Paul at Ephesus and refreshed him, likely delivering the letter that prompted 1 Corinthians (1 Cor. 16:17-18). Paul urges the Corinthian church to recognize such men for their service.

name: Parmasta
dictNote: Parmashta was one of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews of Susa in self-defense on the day appointed for their destruction (Esther 9:9).

name: Sorek
dictNote: Choice vine, the name of a valley, i.e., a torrent-bed, now the Wady Surar, “valley of the fertile spot,” which drains the western Judean hills, and flowing by Makkedah and Jabneel, falls into the sea some eight miles south of Joppa. This was the home of Deliah, whom Samson loved (Judg. 16:4).

name: Chiun
note: properly, a statue, i.e. idol; but used (by euphemism) for some heathen deity (perhaps corresponding to Priapus or Baal-peor)
dictNote: Chiun was an astral deity, likely identifying the planet Saturn, whose image the prophet Amos says the Israelites carried and worshipped during the wilderness period (Amos 5:26). The Septuagint rendered the name as Rephan or Remphan, the form Stephen uses when quoting the verse in Acts 7:43. Star worship of this kind was widespread across the ancient Near East, and Assyrian astrological texts record Saturn's association with an underworld deity under a related name.

name: Dilean
dictNote: (gourd), one of the cities in the lowlands of Judah. (Joshua 15:38) It has not been identified with certainty.

name: Matri

secondTemple.excerpt: When the Hebrews had so done, the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin: and when the lot was cast for the families of this tribe, that which was called Matri was taken: and when the lot was cast for the single persons of that family; Saul the son of Kish was taken, for their King.

dictNote: Matri was the family within the tribe of Benjamin to which Saul belonged, named when Saul was chosen by lot to be Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:21). Nothing further is recorded about this family beyond its role in Saul's selection.

name: Mahavite
note: a Machavite or inhabitant of some place named Machaveh

name: Kelaiah
dictNote: Kelaiah, also called Kelita, was a Levite among those who had married foreign wives during the postexilic period and agreed to separate from them under Ezra's reform (Ezra 10:23). A Levite named Kelita later helped the people understand the reading of the law in Nehemiah 8:7, likely the same man.

name: Zethar
dictNote: Zethar was one of the seven eunuchs who attended King Ahasuerus and was sent to bring Queen Vashti before the king's guests, a summons she refused, setting off the events that led to Esther's rise (Esther 1:10-12).

name: Hagab
dictNote: Hagab's descendants, the Bene-Hagab, were among the temple servants, the Nethinim, who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:43-46). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Nahamani
dictNote: Nahamani was one of the leaders of the Jewish community who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, named in the roster of returnees in Nehemiah 7:7. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Kattath
dictNote: (Josh. 19:15), a town of Asher, has been identified with Kana el Jelil. (See CANA.)

name: Adria
dictNote: Adria, or the sea of Adria, refers to the central Mediterranean waters between Crete, Sicily, and Malta through which Paul's ship drifted during the storm before his shipwreck (Acts 27:27). In the first century the term covered this broader stretch of sea rather than only the modern Adriatic between Italy and the Balkans.

name: Alian
dictNote: Alian, also called Alvan, was a son of Shobal and a Horite clan chief in the region of Seir, listed in the genealogy of Edom's earlier inhabitants (Genesis 36:23). Nothing further is known of him.

name: Sharonite
note: a Sharonite or inhabitant of Sharon
dictNote: (belonging to Sharon), The Shitrai, who had charge of the royal herds in the plain of Sharon, (1 Chronicles 27:29) is the only Sharonite mentioned in the Bible.

name: Hasbadana
dictNote: Hasbadana was one of the men who stood beside Ezra on the wooden platform built for the public reading of the law after the return from exile (Nehemiah 8:4). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Crescens
dictNote: Crescens was a coworker of Paul who had gone to Galatia by the time Paul wrote his final letter from Roman imprisonment, one of several companions Paul mentions as having departed (2 Tim. 4:10). Later church tradition, not attested in scripture, associates him with founding churches in Gaul.

name: Zeboim

secondTemple.excerpt: And they took captive Sodom and Adam  and Zeboim, and they took captive Lot also, the son of Abram's brother, and all his possessions, and they went to Dan.  24.

And in this month the Lord executed his judgments on Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Zeboim,  and all the region of the Jordan, and He burned them with fire and brimstone, and destroyed them until this day, even as [lo] I have declared unto thee all their works, that they are wicked and sinners exceedingly, an

dictNote: Gazelles or roes. (1.) One of the “five cities of the plain” of Sodom, generally coupled with Admah (Gen. 10:19; 14:2; Deut. 29:23; Hos. 11:8). It had a king of its own (Shemeber), and was therefore a place of some importance. It was destroyed along with the other cities of the plain. (2.) A valley or rugged glen somewhere near Gibeah in Benjamin (1 Sam. 13:18). It was probably the ravine now bearing the name Wady Shakh-ed-Dub’a, or “ravine of the hyena,” north of Jericho. (3.) A place mentioned only in Neh. 11:34, inhabited by the Benjamites after the Captivity.

name: Baal-hamon
dictNote: Place of a multitude, a place where Solomon had an extensive vineyard (Cant. 8:11). It has been supposed to be identical with Baal-gad, and also with Hammon in the tribe of Asher (Josh. 19:28). Others identify it with Belamon, in Central Palestine, near Dothaim.

name: Sychem
note: Sychem (i.e. Shekem), the name of a Canaanite and of a place in Palestine
dictNote: See SHECHEM.

name: Saph
dictNote: A Philistine giant of the line of the Rephaim, killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite during a battle with the Philistines at Gob; the parallel genealogical account in Chronicles calls him Sippai (2 Samuel 21:18; 1 Chronicles 20:4).

name: Tiberius
note: The emperor whose fifteenth regnal year dates the start of John's ministry (3:1) — the same verse that names Pilate, Herod, Philip, and Lysanias all at once. Josephus's own account of Tiberius's court, years later, follows the Herodian family Agrippa grew up inside of — the same royal household Luke's chronology is built around.

secondTemple.excerpt: Agrippa lived at Rome: and was generally brought up and conversed with Drusus, the Emperor Tiberius's son: and contracted a friendship with Antonia, the wife of Drusus the Great.

dictNote: (in full, Tiberius Claudius Nero), the second Roman emperor, successor of Augustus, who began to reign A.D. 14 and reigned until A.D. 37. He was the son of Tiberius Claudius Nero and Livia, and hence a stepson of Augustus. He was born at Rome on the 18th of November, B.C. 45. He became emperor in his fifty-fifth year, after having distinguished himself as a commander in various wars, and having evinced talents of a high order as an orator and an administrator of civil affairs. He even gained the reputation of possessing the sterner virtues of the Roman character, and was regarded as entirely worthy of the imperial honors to which his birth and supposed personal merits at length opened the way. Yet, on being raised to the supreme power, he suddenly became, or showed himself to be a very different man. His subsequent life was one of inactivity, sloth and self-indulgence. He was despotic in his government, cruel and vindictive in his disposition. He died A.D. 37, at the age of 78, after a reign of twenty-three years. Our Saviour was put to death in the reign of Tiberius.

name: Quirinius
note: Named once, for the census that gets Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem (2:2) — Cyrenius in the old spelling. Josephus opens the very next book of his own history with the same man's arrival in Syria to do exactly that job: take an account of the province's substance for Rome.

secondTemple.excerpt: Now Cyrenius, a Roman senator, and one who had gone through other magistracies, and had passed through them till he had been consul… came at this time into Syria… being sent by Cesar to be a judge of that nation, and to take an account of their substance.

name: Asshurim
note: an Ashurite (collectively) or inhabitant of Ashur, a district in Palestine

name: Abagtha
dictNote: Abagtha was one of the seven eunuchs who served in the court of King Ahasuerus and was sent to summon Queen Vashti to display her beauty before the king's guests, a command she refused (Esther 1:10-12).

name: Amam
dictNote: (gathering place), a city in the south of Judah named with Shema and Moladah in (Joshua 15:26) only.

name: Gebim
dictNote: Cisterns, (rendered “pits,” Jer. 14:3; “locusts,” Isa. 33:4), a small place north of Jerusalem, whose inhabitants fled at the approach of the Assyrian army (Isa. 10:31). It is probably the modern el-Isawiyeh.

name: Salamis

dictNote: A city on the south-east coast of Cyprus (Acts 13:5), where Saul and Barnabas, on their first missionary journey, preached the word in one of the Jewish synagogues, of which there seem to have been several in that place. It is now called Famagusta.

name: Jambres

secondTemple.excerpt: Bernard informs us here, that instead of this single priest or prophet of the Egyptians, without a name in Josephus, the Targum of Jonathan names the two famous antagonists of Moses, Jannes and Jambres.

dictNote: Jambres, along with Jannes, was one of two Egyptian magicians tradition names as having opposed Moses before Pharaoh, replicating some of the plague signs through their secret arts (compare Exodus 7:11, 22). Paul cites the pair by name in 2 Timothy 3:8 as an example of men who oppose the truth, drawing on a tradition current among Jewish teachers though not recorded by name in the Old Testament text itself.

name: Admatha
dictNote: Admatha was one of seven princes of Persia and Media who had access to the king and sat first in the kingdom, consulted by Ahasuerus after Queen Vashti's refusal to appear before him (Esther 1:14).

name: Shaashgaz
dictNote: Shaashgaz was the eunuch in charge of the king's concubines in the harem of Ahasuerus, responsible for the women, including Esther, after their first night with the king (Esther 2:14).

name: Myra
note: Myra, a place in Asia Minor
dictNote: One of the chief towns of Lycia, in Asia Minor, about 2 1/2 miles from the coast (Acts 27:5). Here Paul removed from the Adramyttian ship in which he had sailed from Caesarea, and entered into the Alexandrian ship, which was afterwards wrecked at Melita (27:39-44).

name: Elika
dictNote: Elika was a Harodite listed among David's mighty men in 2 Samuel 23:25. He does not appear in the parallel list of mighty men in 1 Chronicles 11, one of several names that differ between the two rosters.

name: Pethor
dictNote: Interpretation of dreams, identified with Pitru, on the west bank of the Euphrates, a few miles south of the Hittite capital of Carchemish (Num. 22:5, “which is by the river of the land of the children of [the god] Ammo”). (See BALAAM.)

name: Resen
dictNote: Head of the stream; bridle, one of Nimrod’s cities (Gen. 10:12), “between Nineveh and Calah.” It has been supposed that the four cities named in this verse were afterwards combined into one under the name of Nineveh (q.v.). Resen was on the east side of the Tigris. It is probably identified with the mound of ruins called Karamless.

name: Baharumite
note: a Bacharumite or inhabitant of Bachurim

name: Ethni
dictNote: Ethni was a Gershonite Levite listed in the genealogy of the musician Asaph in 1 Chronicles 6:41. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Asherites
note: an Asherite (collectively) or descendant of Asher
dictNote: descendants of Asher, and members of his tribe. (Judges 1:32)

name: Heresh
dictNote: A Levite listed among those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile, one of the temple gatekeepers descended from the guild of singers (1 Chronicles 9:15).

name: Tahrea
dictNote: A great-grandson of Saul through Jonathan and Mephibosheth, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin preserved after the exile (1 Chronicles 9:41); the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 8:35 gives his name as Tarea.

name: Maadiah
dictNote: A priest who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and headed one of the priestly families reorganized under Joiakim; the same family is called Moadiah a few verses later (Nehemiah 12:5, 17).

name: Pildash
dictNote: One of the eight sons born to Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his wife Milcah, part of a genealogy that connects Abraham's extended family to Aram (Genesis 22:20-22).

name: Suah
dictNote: A descendant of Asher listed among the sons of Zophah in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:36.

name: Hadad

dictNote: Hadad was a common name among Edomite kings and also the name of an Edomite prince who fled to Egypt as a child when David's forces conquered Edom, later returning as an adversary who troubled Solomon's reign.

name: Esek
dictNote: Esek is not a person but a well that Isaac's herdsmen dug in the valley of Gerar; the name means "contention" or "quarrel," because Philistine herdsmen from Gerar disputed Isaac's claim to the water (Genesis 26:20). It was the first of three wells dug during that dispute, the others being Sitnah and the uncontested Rehoboth.

name: Marsena
dictNote: One of the seven princes of Persia and Media named as royal counselors to Ahasuerus, advisers who had direct access to the king and the highest seats in the kingdom (Esther 1:14).

name: Shimon
dictNote: A man of Judah whose four sons appear in a brief, otherwise unexplained genealogical note in 1 Chronicles 4:20.

name: Canneh
dictNote: Mentioned only in Ezek. 27:23. (See CALNEH.)

name: Jehudijah
dictNote: Not actually a personal name: the Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles 4:18 reads "ha-Yehudiyyah," an epithet meaning "the Jewess," attached to one of the wives of Mered in the genealogy of Judah. Many interpreters identify her with Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, named in the same verse, whose marriage into Judah's line made her "the Jewess" by adoption rather than birth.

name: Patara
note: Patara, a place in Asia Minor
dictNote: A city on the south-west coast of Lycia at which Paul landed on his return from his third missionary journey (Acts 21:1, 2). Here he found a larger vessel, which was about to sail across the open sea to the coast of Phoenicia. In this vessel he set forth, and reached the city of Tyre in perhaps two or three days.

name: Linus
dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul names in his greetings to Timothy (2 Timothy 4:21). Early church tradition, recorded by Irenaeus, identifies him as the first bishop of Rome after Peter and Paul, though the New Testament itself says nothing about any church office he held.

name: Jahzerah
dictNote: A priest in the genealogy of those who resettled Jerusalem after the exile, son of Meshullam and father of Adiel (1 Chronicles 9:12); the parallel list in Nehemiah 11:13 gives the name as Ahzai.

name: Terah
note: Abraham's father, named once in the genealogy (3:34). Josephus gives him an actual date — 292 years after the flood — trying to pin Genesis's long lifespans to a real chronology, the same impulse behind Luke's own carefully unbroken chain.

secondTemple.excerpt: Terah begat Abram in his seventieth year… Terah: who was the father of Abraham: who accordingly was the tenth from Noah: and was born in the two hundred and ninety second year after the deluge.

dictNote: Terah was Abraham's father, and Genesis records that he set out from Ur with Abraham, Abraham's wife Sarah, and his grandson Lot, intending to reach Canaan, but the family settled in Haran instead and Terah died there, leaving Abraham to complete the journey after God's call came to him directly.

name: Damascene
note: a Damascene or inhabitant of Damascus

name: Chub
dictNote: Chub is not a person but a people named once, in Ezekiel's oracle against Egypt, among the nations allied with Egypt that would fall by the sword (Ezekiel 30:5). Their identity is uncertain; many scholars suspect textual corruption and would read "Lub," meaning Libya, already named in the same list, though the reading is disputed.

name: Ahasbai
dictNote: Father of Eliphelet, one of David's mighty men listed in the roster of 2 Samuel 23:34; the parallel roster in 1 Chronicles 11:35 gives a garbled form of the same family line as Ur and Eliphal.

name: Gunites
note: a Gunite (collectively with article prefix) or descendants of Guni

name: Aroerite
note: an Aroerite or inhabitant of Aroer
dictNote: Hothan the Aroerite was the father of two of David’s captains. (1 Chronicles 11:44)

name: Melita
note: Melita, an island in the Mediterranean
dictNote: Melita is not a person but the ancient name of Malta, the island in the central Mediterranean where Paul's ship ran aground during the storm recorded in Acts 27. Long settled by Phoenicians and later held by Carthage and then Rome, Malta preserves Phoenician and Punic remains, including bilingual inscriptions, from this era. Paul and his companions spent three months on the island before completing the voyage to Rome (Acts 28:1-11).

name: Jahmai
dictNote: A head of a family within the house of Tolah, one of the clans of Issachar counted as fighting men in David's day (1 Chronicles 7:2).

name: Elnaam
dictNote: Father of two of David's mighty men, Jeribai and Joshaviah, named in the expanded roster of David's warriors in 1 Chronicles 11:46.

name: Jeezer
dictNote: Head of the Manassite clan of the Jeezerites counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:30); the same name appears elsewhere as Abiezer, the fuller form from which Gideon's own clan later descended (Judges 6:11).

name: Janna
dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy, between Joseph and Melchi (Luke 3:24); some manuscripts and the Revised Version spell the name Jannai.

name: Darda

dictNote: One of four men renowned for wisdom before Solomon's time, named as a standard of proverbial wisdom that Solomon was said to exceed (1 Kings 4:31); the same name appears again among the sons of Zerah in 1 Chronicles 2:6.

note: a Jakinite (collectively) or descendants of Jakin

name: Likhi
dictNote: A descendant of Manasseh through Shemidah, listed among the family heads of that tribe (1 Chronicles 7:19).

name: Tehinnah
dictNote: A descendant of Judah credited as the founder of Ir-nahash, "city of Nahash," named in the tribal genealogies of Judah (1 Chronicles 4:12).

name: Shachia (from the margin)
dictNote: A son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh, born in Moab and listed among the heads of families in Benjamin's genealogy (1 Chronicles 8:8-10).

name: Salim
dictNote: Peaceful, a place near AEnon (q.v.), on the west of Jordan, where John baptized (John 3:23). It was probably the Shalem mentioned in Gen. 33:18, about 7 miles south of AEnon, at the head of the great Wady Far’ah, which formed the northern boundary of Judea in the Jordan valley.

name: Zia
dictNote: A head of a family in the tribe of Gad, listed among those settled in Bashan (1 Chronicles 5:13).

name: Secacah
dictNote: Enclosure, one of the six cities in the wilderness of Judah, noted for its “great cistern” (Josh. 15:61). It has been identified with the ruin Sikkeh, east of Bethany.

name: Maoch
dictNote: Father of Achish, the Philistine king of Gath who sheltered David from Saul (1 Samuel 27:2). A later king of Gath also named Achish, son of Maacah, appears in Solomon's reign (1 Kings 2:39); whether Maoch and Maacah are the same figure or the name simply recurred in Gath's ruling house is uncertain.

name: Berites
note: (only in the plural and with the article) the Berites, a place in Palestine

name: Colosse
note: Colossæ, a place in Asia Minor
dictNote: more properly Colos’sae, was a city of Phrygia in Asia Minor, in the upper part of the basin of the Maeander, on the Lycus. Hierapolis and Laodicea were in its immediate neighborhood. dictNote: The name given to the new and mixed inhabitants whom Esarhaddon (B.C. 677), the king of Assyria, brought from Babylon and other places and settled in the cities of Samaria, instead of the original inhabitants whom Sargon (B.C. 721) had removed into captivity (2 Kings 17:24; comp. Ezra 4:2, 9, 10). These strangers (comp. Luke 17:18) amalgamated with the Jews still remaining in the land, and gradually abandoned their old idolatry and adopted partly the Jewish religion. After the return from the Captivity, the Jews in Jerusalem refused to allow them to take part with them in rebuilding the temple, and hence sprang up an open enmity between them. They erected a rival temple on Mount Gerizim, which was, however, destroyed by a Jewish king (B.C. 130). They then built another at Shechem. The bitter enmity between the Jews and Samaritans continued in the time of our Lord: the Jews had “no dealings with the Samaritans” (John 4:9; comp. Luke 9:52, 53). Our Lord was in contempt called “a Samaritan” (John 8:48). Many of the Samaritans early embraced the gospel (John 4:5-42; Acts 8:25; 9:31; 15:3). Of these Samaritans there still remains a small population of about one hundred and sixty, who all reside in Shechem, where they carefully observe the religious customs of their fathers. They are the “smallest and oldest sect in the world.”

name: Joelah
dictNote: One of the Benjamite warriors, kinsmen of Saul's own tribe, who defected to join David while he was still an outlaw at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:7).

dictNote: (praised), one of the towns of the tribe of Dan, (Joshua 19:45) named between Baalath and Bene-berak.

name: Chesil
dictNote: Ungodly, a town in the south of Judah (Josh. 15:30); probably the same as Bethul (19:4) and Bethuel (1 Chr. 4:30); now Khelasa.

name: Zabud
dictNote: Son of the prophet Nathan, who served Solomon as "the king's friend," a formal court title for a trusted personal adviser (1 Kings 4:5).

name: Ituraea
note: Ituræa (i.e. Jetur), a region of Palestine
dictNote: A district in the north-east of Palestine, forming, along with the adjacent territory of Trachonitis, the tetrarchy of Philip (Luke 3:1). The present Jedur comprehends the chief part of Ituraea. It is bounded on the east by Trachonitis, on the south by Gaulanitis, on the west by Hermon, and on the north by the plain of Damascus.

name: Ispah
dictNote: A head of a Benjamite family descended from Beriah, listed among the clan leaders who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 8:16, 28).

name: Chun
dictNote: One of the cities of Hadarezer, king of Syria. David procured brass (i.e., bronze or copper) from it for the temple (1 Chr. 18:8). It is called Berothai in 2 Sam. 8:8; probably the same as Berothah in Ezek. 47:16.

name: Hazar-susah
dictNote: Village of the horse, the same as Sansannah, one of Solomon’s “chariot cities” (Josh. 15:31; 2 Chr. 1:14), a depot in the south border of Judah.

name: Archevite
note: an Arkevite (collectively) or native of Erek
dictNote: One of the nations planted by the Assyrians in Samaria (Ezra 4:9); the men of Erech.

name: Zebudah

secondTemple.excerpt: Now Jehoiakim’s mother was called Zebudah , of the city Rumah.

dictNote: Wife of King Josiah of Judah and mother of his son Jehoiakim, who succeeded to the throne after the brief reign of his brother Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:36).

name: Kibzaim
dictNote: Two heaps, a city of Ephraim, assigned to the Kohathite Levites, and appointed as a city of refuge (Josh. 21: 22). It is also called Jokmeam (1 Chr. 6:68).

name: Ashima
dictNote: Ashima is not a person but a deity, the god of the people of Hamath whom the Assyrians resettled in Samaria after deporting the northern kingdom's population (2 Kings 17:30). Little is known of the cult beyond this notice; some scholars connect the name to "Ashim-Bethel," a divine name that turns up centuries later among Aramaic-speaking Jews at Elephantine in Egypt.

name: Ephlal
dictNote: A descendant of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel, listed in a genealogy that traces the family through a servant, Jarha, who married into the household (1 Chronicles 2:34-37).

name: Gemalli
dictNote: Father of Ammiel, the representative of the tribe of Dan among the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:12).

name: Sarsechim

dictNote: One of the Babylonian officials present at the fall of Jerusalem, listed among the officers who sat in the middle gate at Nebuchadnezzar's order after the city's walls were breached (Jeremiah 39:3).

name: Agur
note: Agur, a fanciful name for Solomon

name: Dekar
dictNote: Father of Ben-Dekar, one of Solomon's twelve district officers, responsible for supplying the royal household from the region including Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh (1 Kings 4:9).

name: Jaanai
dictNote: A chief among the Gadites who settled in Bashan, named in the tribal record of 1 Chronicles 5:12.

name: Nezib
dictNote: A town in the “plain” of Judah. It has been identified with Beit Nuzib, about 14 miles south-west of Jerusalem, in the Wady Sur (Josh. 15:43).

name: Seled
dictNote: A descendant of Jerahmeel through Nadab, listed in Judah's genealogy as having died without children (1 Chronicles 2:30).

name: Imna

secondTemple.excerpt: And the sons of Asher: Imnah, and Ishvah, (and Ishvi), and Beriah, and Serah, their one sister--six.

dictNote: Imnah was a son of Asher, listed among the tribal genealogies in Genesis and Numbers.

name: Merodach

secondTemple.excerpt: But now, after the death of Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach his son succeeded in the Kingdom: who immediately set Jechoniah at liberty, and esteemed him among his most intimate friends.

dictNote: Merodach is not a person but Marduk, the chief god of Babylon, invoked in Jeremiah's oracle announcing Babylon's fall: "Merodach is broken in pieces" (Jeremiah 50:2). Marduk's supremacy in Babylonian religion is confirmed by extensive cuneiform sources, including the creation epic Enuma Elish and the Cyrus Cylinder, which credits the god with handing Babylon to Cyrus the Persian, the very event this oracle anticipates.

name: Ishbi-benob (from the margin)
dictNote: One of the descendants of the Rephaim, a Philistine giant who nearly killed David in battle before Abishai intervened and struck him down (2 Samuel 21:16-17). The episode marks the point at which David's men insisted he no longer go out to battle personally.

name: Shavsha
dictNote: One of David's royal secretaries (1 Chronicles 18:16); the same official appears under the names Seraiah in 2 Samuel 8:17, Sheva in 2 Samuel 20:25, and Shisha in 1 Kings 4:3, the variation typical of how court titles and names were transliterated across parallel records.

name: Arcturus
note: the constellation of the Great Bear (perhaps from its migration through the heavens)
dictNote: Arcturus is not a person but the King James rendering of a Hebrew word in Job 9:9 and 38:32 that most likely designates the constellation now called Ursa Major, the Great Bear, rather than the star Arcturus itself; the verses point to God's authority over the fixed courses of the constellations.

name: Diotrephes
note: Jove-nourished; Diotrephes, an opponent of Christianity
dictNote: A leader in a local church rebuked by John for loving to be first, refusing to welcome traveling missionaries, and spreading malicious accusations against John and his coworkers, even expelling members who did welcome them (3 John 1:9-10).

name: Ahinadab
dictNote: One of Solomon's twelve district officers, assigned to Mahanaim east of the Jordan, responsible for supplying provisions to the royal household one month each year (1 Kings 4:14).

name: Jahzeelites
note: a Jachtseelite (collectively) or descendants of Jachtseel

name: Baaseiah
dictNote: A Levite ancestor of Asaph, David's chief musician, named in the genealogy tracing Asaph's line back through the Kohathite branch of Levi (1 Chronicles 6:25-40).

name: Goath
dictNote: A lowing, a place near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Jer. 31:39.

name: Muppim

secondTemple.excerpt: And the sons of Benjamin: Bela and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, and Ehi, and Rosh, and Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard--eleven.

dictNote: One of the sons of Benjamin who went to Egypt with Jacob's household, listed in Genesis 46:21; the parallel census in Numbers 26:39 gives the name as Shupham, head of the Shuphamite clan.

name: Shichemites
note: a Shikmite (collectively), or descendants of Shekem

name: Tirathite
note: a Tirathite or inhabitant of an unknown Tirah

name: Jonan
dictNote: An ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy, listed as the son of Eliakim (Luke 3:30).

name: Rhodes

Paul's ship stopped there briefly on his return from his third missionary journey (Acts 21:1).

name: Tel-abib
dictNote: Hill of corn, a place on the river Chebar, the residence of Ezekiel (Ezek. 3:15). The site is unknown.

name: Mnason
dictNote: A Christian from Cyprus, described as an "early disciple," meaning he had been a believer since the earliest days of the Jerusalem church; Paul and his companions stayed at his house in Jerusalem near the end of the third missionary journey (Acts 21:16).

name: Jozachar
dictNote: One of two court officials who assassinated King Joash of Judah at Beth-millo, in retaliation, according to Chronicles, for the killing of the priest Zechariah (2 Kings 12:20-21); the parallel account in 2 Chronicles 24:26 calls him Zabad.

name: Jairite
note: a Jairite or descendant of Jair
dictNote: (descendant of Jair). The Ira THE JAIRITE was a priest (Authorized Version “chief ruler”) to David (2 Samuel 20:26)

name: Sibraim
dictNote: (twofold hope), one of the landmarks on the northern boundary of the holy land as stated by Ezekiel. (Ezekiel 47:16) It has not been identified.

name: Balah
dictNote: A city in the tribe of Simeon (Josh. 19:3), elsewhere called Bilhah (1 Chr. 4:29) and Baalah (Josh. 15:29).

name: Salmon
dictNote: A Hebrew strong-number variant tied to the same verse pair as the entry above; refers to the same man, son of Nahshon, father of Boaz by Rahab, and ancestor of David and of Jesus through Matthew's genealogy (Ruth 4:20-21; Matthew 1:4-5).

name: Shoham
dictNote: A Merarite Levite, son of Jaaziah, listed among the Levitical divisions organized for temple service under David (1 Chronicles 24:26-27).

name: Pharaoh-hophra
dictNote: Pharaoh Hophra, known to history as Apries, ruled Egypt from about 589 to 570 BC and briefly supported King Zedekiah of Judah's revolt against Babylon before withdrawing, leaving Jerusalem to fall in 586 BC. Jeremiah predicted that Hophra, like Zedekiah, would be handed over to his enemies (Jeremiah 44:30); Egyptian records confirm he was overthrown in a civil war led by his general Amasis and later killed, a case where a specific biblical prophecy about a named foreign king's downfall is corroborated by that king's own country's records.

name: Jushab-hesed
dictNote: One of the sons of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the first group of exiles back from Babylon to rebuild the temple, listed in the royal genealogy of Judah after the exile (1 Chronicles 3:20).

name: Idbash
dictNote: One of three sons of the father of Etam, listed in the tribal genealogy of Judah alongside his sister Hazelelponi (1 Chronicles 4:3).

name: Zephon
dictNote: A son of Gad and head of the clan of the Zephonites counted in the wilderness census (Numbers 26:15); the earlier list in Genesis 46:16 spells the name Ziphion.

name: Sansannah
dictNote: A palm branch, or a thorn bush, a town in the south (the negeb) of Judah (Josh. 15:31); called also Hazarsusah (19:5), or Hazar-susim (1 Chr. 4:31).

name: Parshandatha
dictNote: The eldest of Haman's ten sons, killed by the Jews of Susa along with his brothers when they defended themselves against the pogrom Haman had planned (Esther 9:7-10).

name: Illyricum
note: (the) Illyrican (shore), i.e. (as a name itself) Illyricum, a region of Europe
dictNote: A country to the north-west of Macedonia, on the eastern shores of the Adriatic, now almost wholly comprehended in Dalmatia, a name formerly given to the southern part of Illyricum (2 Tim. 4:10). It was traversed by Paul in his third missionary journey (Rom. 15:19). It was the farthest district he had reached in preaching the gospel of Christ. This reference to Illyricum is in harmony with Acts 20:2, inasmuch as the apostle’s journey over the parts of Macedonia would bring him to the borders of Illyricum.

name: Hasrah
dictNote: Keeper of the sacred vestments in the temple and husband of Huldah the prophetess, whom King Josiah's officials consulted after the Book of the Law was discovered (2 Chronicles 34:22); the parallel account in 2 Kings 22:14 gives his name as Harhas.

name: Amasiah
dictNote: A commander of thousands in the army of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, listed among the officers who volunteered themselves for the LORD's service in the military reorganization of 2 Chronicles 17:16. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Heli
dictNote: Named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the father of Joseph (Luke 3:23), though Matthew's genealogy names Jacob as Joseph's father instead. Since antiquity, readers have proposed that Luke traces Mary's ancestry through Heli while Matthew traces Joseph's, or that the two lists reflect a levirate marriage; the discrepancy is old and remains unresolved. Nothing else concerning Heli is recorded in scripture.

name: Jeremai
dictNote: One of the men descended from Hashum listed among those who had married foreign wives during the postexilic community and agreed, under Ezra's direction, to separate from them (Ezra 10:33). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Seirath
dictNote: Woody district; shaggy, a place among the mountains of Ephraim, bordering on Benjamin, to which Ehud fled after he had assassinated Eglon at Jericho (Judg. 3:26, 27).

name: Gederathite
note: a Gederathite, or inhabitant of Gederah
dictNote: An epithet applied to Josabad, one of David’s warriors at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:4), a native of Gederah.

name: Abiud
dictNote: Listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as a descendant of Zerubbabel, in the line leading from the Babylonian exile to Joseph (Matt. 1:13). He does not appear in Luke's parallel genealogy, and nothing about his life is otherwise recorded.

name: Beth-haran
note: Beth-ha-Ran, a place East of the Jordan
dictNote: (Numbers 32:36) It is no doubt the same place as BETH-ARAM. (Joshua 13:27)

name: Chenani
dictNote: A Levite who stood on the stairs with several others and cried out to the LORD during the great public confession and covenant renewal described in Nehemiah 9, following the reading of the Law under Ezra. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Zibia
dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the descendants of Shaharaim in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:9. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Sadoc

dictNote: Called also Azzah, which is its Hebrew name (Deut. 2:23; 1 Kings 4:24; Jer. 25:20), strong, a city on the Mediterranean shore, remarkable for its early importance as the chief centre of a great commercial traffic with Egypt. It is one of the oldest cities of the world (Gen. 10:19; Josh. 15:47). Its earliest inhabitants were the Avims, who were conquered and displaced by the Caphtorims (Deut. 2:23; Josh. 13:2, 3), a Philistine tribe. In the division of the land it fell to the lot of Judah (Josh. 15:47; Judg. 1:18). It was the southernmost of the five great Philistine cities which gave each a golden emerod as a trespass-offering unto the Lord (1 Sam. 6:17). Its gates were carried away by Samson (Judg. 16:1-3). Here he was afterwards a prisoner, and “did grind in the prison house.” Here he also pulled down the temple of Dagon, and slew “all the lords of the Philistines,” himself also perishing in the ruin (Judg. 16:21-30). The prophets denounce the judgments of God against it (Jer. 25:20; 47:5; Amos 1:6, 7; Zeph. 2:4). It is referred to in Acts 8:26. Philip is here told to take the road from Jerusalem to Gaza (about 6 miles south-west of Jerusalem), “which is desert”, i.e., the “desert road,” probably by Hebron, through the desert hills of Southern Judea. (See SAMSON.) It is noticed on monuments as early as B.C. 1600. Its small port is now called el-Mineh.

name: Biztha
dictNote: One of the seven eunuchs who served in the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus, likely Xerxes I, sent to bring Queen Vashti before the king's banquet, a summons she refused (Esther 1:10-12). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

name: Gilalai
dictNote: One of the priests' sons who played musical instruments in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls under Nehemiah (Neh. 12:36). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Hodaiah
dictNote: A descendant of the royal line of Judah listed among the sons of Elioenai in the genealogies following the Babylonian exile (1 Chr. 3:24). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Telaim
dictNote: Young lambs, a place at which Saul gathered his army to fight against Amalek (1 Sam. 15:4); probably the same as Telem (2).

dictNote: A Christian in Rome to whom Paul sends greetings near the close of his letter to the Romans, grouped with Asyncritus, Hermas, Patrobas, and Hermes (Rom. 16:14). Nothing further about him is recorded.

name: Beth-tappuah
dictNote: House of apples, a town of Judah, now Tuffuh, 5 miles west of Hebron (Josh. 15:53).

name: Zemira
dictNote: A Benjamite, one of the sons of Becher, listed among the heads of families noted for their military strength in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:8. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Jekuthiel
dictNote: Listed in the genealogies of Judah as connected to the town of Zanoah, recorded among the descendants attributed to Mered's Egyptian wife Bithiah (1 Chr. 4:18). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Nohah
dictNote: The fourth son of Benjamin listed in the tribal genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:2. He does not appear in the earlier lists of Benjamin's sons in Genesis or Numbers, and nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Syrophenician
note: a Syro-phœnician woman, i.e. a female native of Phœnicia in Syria
dictNote: Not a personal name but a term for a Gentile of Phoenician descent from the Roman province of Syria, used in Mark 7:26 to describe the woman whose daughter Jesus healed from a distance near Tyre; Matthew's parallel calls her "a woman of Canaan" (Matt. 15:22). The term distinguished Syrian Phoenicians from the Phoenicians of Libya around Carthage. Her persistent faith, despite Jesus's initial refusal, became a byword for Gentile inclusion in the gospel.

name: Jannes

dictNote: One of two Egyptian magicians, remembered in later Jewish tradition as Jannes and Jambres, who imitated Moses's signs before Pharaoh and opposed him, according to 2 Timothy 3:8. Neither man is actually named in Exodus itself; Paul draws on a well-known tradition as an example of false teachers who resist the truth.

name: Beeliada
dictNote: One of David's sons born in Jerusalem, listed in 1 Chronicles 14:7; the parallel lists in 2 Samuel 5:16 and 1 Chronicles 3:8 call him Eliada instead, Beeliada apparently being an earlier form of the name later avoided because it contained the element "Baal."

dictNote: Not a person but the great capital of Lower Egypt, called Moph in Hosea 9:6 and Noph elsewhere (Isa. 19:13; Jer. 2:16, 46:14; Ezek. 30:13-16), located on the west bank of the Nile near modern Cairo. Founded according to tradition by Menes, Egypt's first king, it served as a major religious and political center for centuries. Its ruins, including a colossal fallen statue of Ramesses II, lie near the village of Mit Rahina and are recognized today, along with the nearby pyramid fields of Saqqara, as a UNESCO World Heritage site.

name: Nakbi
dictNote: One of the twelve tribal representatives Moses sent to spy out the land of Canaan, representing the tribe of Naphtali and identified as the son of Vophsi (Num. 13:14). Along with all but Joshua and Caleb, he returned from the mission with the majority report that discouraged the people from entering the land. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Jachan
dictNote: A chief among the Gadite clans who settled in Bashan, listed among the heads of families in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 5:13. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Ashterathite
note: an Ashterathite or inhabitant of Ashtaroth
dictNote: a native or inhabitant of Ashtaroth, (1 Chronicles 11:44) beyond Jordan.

name: Hoham
dictNote: The Amorite king of Hebron who joined four other Canaanite kings in besieging Gibeon after it made peace with Israel, prompting Joshua's forced march and the battle in which the sun and moon reportedly stood still (Josh. 10:1-27). He and his allied kings were later found hiding in a cave at Makkedah, captured, and executed.

name: Addan
dictNote: Not a person but a place name, one of several Babylonian localities named in Ezra 2:59 (called Addon in the parallel list of Nehemiah 7:61) from which a group of exiles returned to Judah after the exile but could not prove their genealogical descent from Israel. Its exact location is unknown.

name: Achmetha
note: Achmetha (i.e. Ecbatana), the summer capital of Persia
dictNote: Not a person but the Aramaic name in Ezra 6:2 for Ecbatana, the ancient capital of Media and summer residence of the Persian kings, located near modern Hamadan, Iran. The decree of Cyrus authorizing the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple was found archived there, since Cyrus had held court at Ecbatana before later Persian kings shifted their main residence to Susa. Excavations at Hamadan have confirmed continuous occupation from the Median period onward, though the ancient Achaemenid palace itself has not been conclusively located beneath the modern city.

name: Carshena
dictNote: One of the seven highest-ranking princes of Persia and Media, advisers with direct access to King Ahasuerus who were consulted after Queen Vashti refused to appear before him (Esther 1:14). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

name: Poratha
dictNote: One of the ten sons of Haman killed by the Jews of Susa when they defended themselves against the pogrom Haman had planned, as recorded in Esther 9:8. Their deaths are commemorated in the Jewish festival of Purim.

name: Rabbith
dictNote: (multitude) a town in the territory, perhaps on the boundary, of Issachar. (Joshua 18:20) only.

name: Shiphmite
note: a Shiphmite or inhabitant of Shepham
dictNote: Probably the designation of Zabdi, who has charge of David’s vineyards (1 Chr. 27:27).

dictNote: Not a personal name but a term for the nomadic peoples who inhabited the steppes north of the Black Sea and Caspian Sea, proverbial in the ancient world as distant and uncivilized outsiders. Paul uses the term in Colossians 3:11 to list categories erased by unity in Christ, alongside Greek, Jew, barbarian, slave, and free, making the point that the gospel's reach extends even to peoples considered furthest outside civilized society.

name: Ephphatha
dictNote: Not a person but an Aramaic word meaning "be opened," spoken by Jesus when he healed a deaf man with a speech impediment near the Decapolis (Mark 7:34). Mark is noted for preserving several of Jesus's actual Aramaic words in transliterated form, including talitha cumi (Mark 5:41) and his cry from the cross, eloi eloi lama sabachthani (Mark 15:34), details that reflect the eyewitness texture of his gospel.

name: Herodion
dictNote: A Christian in Rome whom Paul greets as his "kinsman," likely meaning a fellow Jew rather than a blood relative, near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom. 16:11). His name, derived from the Herod family, suggests he may have belonged to the household of a member of the Herodian dynasty.

name: Rakkon

name: Gur
dictNote: A whelp, a place near Ibleam where Jehu’s servants overtook and mortally wounded king Ahaziah (2 Kings 9:27); an ascent from the plain of Jezreel.

name: Patrobas

name: Armoni
dictNote: One of two sons of Saul by his concubine Rizpah, handed over by David to the Gibeonites and executed to atone for Saul's earlier slaughter of Gibeonites in violation of Israel's ancient treaty with them (2 Sam. 21:1-9). Rizpah's subsequent vigil guarding his exposed body, and that of his brother Mephibosheth, from scavenging animals became one of the Old Testament's most striking images of grief and finally moved David to give the dead a proper burial.

name: Idumaea

dictNote: The Greek form of Edom (Isa. 34:5, 6; Ezek. 35:15; 36:5, but in R.V. “Edom”). (See EDOM).

name: Eladah
dictNote: An Ephraimite listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7:20, an ancestor of Joshua son of Nun according to the family line given there. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Piram
dictNote: The Amorite king of Jarmuth, one of five Canaanite kings who besieged Gibeon and were defeated by Joshua in the battle remembered for the sun standing still (Josh. 10:3, 23). He was captured with his allies hiding in a cave at Makkedah and put to death.

name: Joannas
dictNote: Listed in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as a descendant of Zerubbabel, in the line traced through Nathan rather than Solomon (Luke 3:27). He does not appear in Matthew's parallel genealogy, and nothing further about him is recorded.

name: Neah
dictNote: Shaking, or settlement, or descent, a town on the east side of Zebulun, not far from Rimmon (Josh. 19:13).

name: Philippian
note: a Philippesian (Philippian), i.e. native of Philippi
dictNote: Not a person but a term for an inhabitant of Philippi, the Roman colony in Macedonia where Paul planted a church. Paul uses it in Philippians 4:15 to recall that the Philippians alone supported him financially in the early days of his ministry after he left Macedonia. It describes the congregation collectively rather than any individual.

dictNote: Ibid., a Moabite town threatened with the sword of the Babylonians (Jer. 48:2).

name: Gaham
dictNote: A son of Abraham's brother Nahor by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants in Genesis 22:24. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Epicurean
note: an Epicurean or follower of Epicurus

secondTemple.excerpt: Now there was one Pompedius, a senator, and one who had gone through almost all posts in the government, but otherwise an Epicurean, and for that reason loved to lead an inactive life.

dictNote: Not a person but a follower of the philosophy founded by Epicurus, who taught that pleasure, understood as freedom from pain and disturbance, was the chief good, and that the gods, if they existed, took no active interest in human affairs. Acts 17:18 records Epicurean philosophers debating Paul in Athens alongside Stoics after he preached about Jesus and the resurrection, part of the setting for his address on the Areopagus.

name: Shahazimah (from the margin)
dictNote: (toward the heights), one of the towns of the allotment of Issachar. (Joshua 10:22) only.

name: Bigtha
dictNote: One of the seven eunuchs of the Persian king Ahasuerus's court sent to summon Queen Vashti to his banquet, a command she refused (Esther 1:10-12). Nothing further is recorded about him individually.

name: Irpeel
dictNote: (God heals), one of the cities of Benjamin. (Joshua 18:27) No trace has yet been discovered of its situation.

name: Raamiah
dictNote: One of the leaders who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel, named in Nehemiah 7:7; the parallel list in Ezra 2:2 calls him Reelaiah instead. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Amminadib
dictNote: A name found only in the King James Version's translation of Song of Solomon 6:12, describing chariots compared to "the chariots of Amminadib." Most modern translations, following the Hebrew more closely, render the phrase differently, as "my noble people" or "the chariots of my people, a prince," treating it as a poetic description rather than a proper name. Whether it refers to an actual individual has long been disputed among translators.

name: Shelanites
note: a Shelanite (collectively), or descendants of Shelah

name: Azmon
dictNote: (strong), a place named as being on the southern boundary of the Holy Land, apparently near the torrent of Egypt (Wadi el-Arish). (Numbers 34:4,5; Joshua 15:4) It has not yet been identified.

name: Tebah
note: Tebach, the name of a Mesopotamian and of an Israelite
dictNote: The eldest son of Abraham's brother Nahor by his concubine Reumah, listed among Nahor's descendants in Genesis 22:24. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Ibnijah
dictNote: A Benjamite listed among the family heads who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 9:8. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Meraiah
dictNote: The head of the priestly family of Seraiah during the high priesthood of Joiakim, listed among the priestly leaders in Nehemiah's record of postexilic priests and Levites (Neh. 12:12). Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Shebarim
dictNote: Breaks; ruins, a place near Ai (Josh. 7:5; R.V. marg., “the quarries”).

name: Nophah
dictNote: Blast, a city of Moab which was occupied by the Amorites (Num. 21:30).

name: Zeri
dictNote: One of the sons of Jeduthun appointed by David to prophesy with musical instruments in the temple service, listed in 1 Chronicles 25:3; he is probably the same man called Izri a few verses later in the same chapter's roster of Levitical musicians (1 Chr. 25:11).

name: Arnan
dictNote: Listed in the genealogy of Zerubbabel's descendants in 1 Chronicles 3:21, continuing the royal line of Judah after the exile. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Moadiah
dictNote: A priestly family head in the postexilic community, named Moadiah in Nehemiah 12:17 and Maadiah in the parallel list of Nehemiah 12:5. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Ishmerai
dictNote: A Benjamite of the family of Elpaal, listed among the heads of families living in Jerusalem in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8:18. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Moloch

secondTemple.excerpt: However, the general sense of both seems to be this: that there were certain chariots, with their horses, dedicated to the idol of the sun, or to Moloch: which idol might be carried about in procession, and worshipped by the people: which chariots were now taken away , as Josephus says: or, as the book of Kings says, burnt with fire by Josiah .

And to this law there is no limit of days, and no remission, nor any atonement: but the man who hath defiled his daughter shall be rooted out in the midst of all Israel, because he hath

given of his seed to Moloch,  and wrought impiously so as to defile it.

dictNote: Not a person but the national god of the Ammonites, worshiped with child sacrifice by fire, also called Molech, Milcom, and Malcham in various Old Testament passages (Lev. 18:21, 20:2-5; 1 Kings 11:5, 33; Zeph. 1:5). Solomon built a high place for Moloch on the Mount of Olives to please his foreign wives, and the cult persisted intermittently until Josiah's reforms destroyed it (1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 23:10, 13). Stephen references the exile-era rebuke of Moloch worship in his speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:43, quoting Amos 5:26); archaeologists have found child burial sites called tophets at Carthage and other Phoenician colonies that many scholars connect to related West Semitic child-sacrifice cults, though the practice's exact nature remains debated.

name: Chesed

secondTemple.excerpt: Now Nahor had eight sons by Milcha; Uz, and Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Azau, Pheldas, Jadelph, and Bethuel.

dictNote: A son of Abraham's brother Nahor, listed among his descendants in Genesis 22:22. Some scholars connect his name to the Hebrew term for the Chaldeans (Kasdim), suggesting later tradition saw him as an ancestor of that people, though the text itself states only his place in Nahor's family.

name: Nedabiah
dictNote: One of the sons of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) of Judah, born either before or during his exile in Babylon, listed in the royal genealogy of 1 Chronicles 3:18. Nothing further is recorded about him.

name: Raca
note: O empty one, i.e. thou worthless (as a term of utter vilification)
dictNote: Not a person but an Aramaic term of contempt, roughly meaning "empty-headed" or "worthless," that Jesus names in the Sermon on the Mount as an insult serious enough to warrant judgment, alongside anger and the word "fool" (Matt. 5:22). His point was that contemptuous words toward another person carry real moral weight, not only physical violence.

name: Pavement
note: stone-strewed, i.e. a tessellated mosaic on which the Roman tribunal was placed
dictNote: Not a person but an elevated, stone-paved platform outside Pilate's headquarters in Jerusalem, called Gabbatha in Aramaic, where Roman governors set up the judgment seat to hear cases in public (John 19:13). It was here that Pilate presented Jesus to the crowd and formally handed him over for crucifixion. Its precise location within ancient Jerusalem has not been conclusively identified, though several sites near the Temple Mount have been proposed.

name: Shiggaion
note: properly, aberration, i.e. (technically) a dithyramb or rambling poem
dictNote: Not a person but a Hebrew musical or poetic term found in the title of Psalm 7, and in its plural form, shigionoth, in Habakkuk 3:1, likely describing an irregular, emotionally intense style of composition, possibly connected to a root meaning "to wander" or "to reel." Its precise musical meaning is uncertain, since no other ancient source explains the term.

name: Silla

secondTemple.excerpt: Who had seventy seven children by two wives, Silla and Ada.

dictNote: A highway; a twig, only in 2 Kings 12:20. If taken as a proper name (as in the LXX. and other versions), the locality is unknown.

name: Harnepher
dictNote: A chief of the tribe of Asher (1 Chr. 7:36).

name: Phanuel

secondTemple.excerpt: But Jacob was pleased with these things; and named the place Phanuel : which signifies The face of God .

dictNote: Face of God, father of the prophetess Anna (q.v.), Luke 2:36.

name: Iron

secondTemple.excerpt: In this ridge of mountains there is one called the Iron mountain , that runs in length as far as Moab.

dictNote: Tubal-Cain is the first-mentioned worker in iron (Gen. 4:22). The Egyptians wrought it at Sinai before the Exodus. David prepared it in great abundance for the temple (1 Chr. 22:3: 29:7). The merchants of Dan and Javan brought it to the market of Tyre (Ezek. 27:19). Various instruments are mentioned as made of iron (Deut. 27:5; 19:5; Josh. 17:16, 18; 1 Sam. 17:7; 2 Sam. 12:31; 2 Kings 6:5, 6; 1 Chr. 22:3; Isa. 10:34). Figuratively, a yoke of iron (Deut. 28:48) denotes hard service; a rod of iron (Ps. 2:9), a stern government; a pillar of iron (Jer. 1:18), a strong support; a furnace of iron (Deut. 4:20), severe labour; a bar of iron (Job 40:18), strength; fetters of iron (Ps. 107:10), affliction; giving silver for iron (Isa. 60:17), prosperity.

name: Mibhar
dictNote: Choice, a Hagarene, one of David’s warriors (1 Chr. 11:38); called also Bani the Gadite (2 Sam. 23:36).

name: Jerubbesheth
note: Jerubbesheth, a symbolic name for Gideon
dictNote: Contender with the shame; i.e., idol, a surname also of Gideon (2 Sam. 11:21).

name: Nebai (from the margin)
dictNote: (fruitful), a family of the heads of the people who signed the covenant with Nehemiah. (Nehemiah 10:19)

name: Tubal-cain
dictNote: The son of Lamech and Zillah, “an instructor of every artificer in brass and iron” (Gen. 4:22; R.V., “the forger of every cutting instrument of brass and iron”).

name: Sceva
dictNote: An implement, a Jew, chief of the priests at Ephesus (Acts 19:13-16); i.e., the head of one of the twenty-four courses of the house of Levi. He had seven sons, who “took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus,” in imitation of Paul. They tried their method of exorcism on a fierce demoniac, and failed. His answer to them was to this effect (19:15): “The Jesus whom you invoke is One whose authority I acknowledge; and the Paul whom you name I recognize to be a servant or messenger of God; but what sort of men are ye who have been empowered to act as you do by neither?” (Lindsay on the Acts of the Apostles.)

name: Ophni
note: an Ophnite (collectively) or inhabitants of Ophen
dictNote: Mouldy, a city of Benjamin (Josh. 18:24).

name: Heleb
dictNote: Fatness, one of David’s warriors (2 Sam. 23:29).

name: Horam
dictNote: (mountainous), king of Gezer at the time of the conquest of the southwestern part of Palestine. (Joshua 10:33)

name: Ethanim
note: Ethanim, the name of a month
dictNote: The month of gifts, i.e., of vintage offerings; called Tisri after the Exile; corresponding to part of September and October. It was the first month of the civil year, and the seventh of the sacred year (1 Kings 8:2).

name: Sabean
note: a Sebaite, or inhabitant of Seba

name: Sabean
note: a Shebaite or descendant of Sheba

name: Shebah
dictNote: (an oath), the famous well which gave its name to the city of Beersheba. (Genesis 26:53) [Beersheba, Or Beersheba]

name: Reumah
dictNote: (elevated), the concubine of Nahor, Abraham’s brother. (Genesis 22:4) (B.C. about 1870.)

name: Bamah
dictNote: A height, a name used simply to denote a high place where the Jews worshipped idols (Ezek. 20:29). The plural is translated “high places” in Num. 22:41 and Ezek. 36:2.

name: Maai
dictNote: (compassionate), one of the Bene-Asaph who took part in the solemn musical service by which the wall of Jerusalem was dedicated. (Nehemiah 12:36)

name: Rakkath
dictNote: Shore-town, a “fenced city” of the tribe of Naphtali (Josh. 19:35). The old name of Tiberias, according to the Rabbins.

name: Stoick
note: a "Stoic" (as occupying a particular porch in Athens), i.e. adherent of a certin philosophy

name: Mattathah
dictNote: (gift of Jehovah), probably a contraction of Mattathiah.

name: Moresheth-gath
dictNote: Possession of the wine-press, the birthplace of the prophet Micah (1:14), who is called the “Morasthite” (Jer. 26:18). This place was probably a suburb of Gath.

name: Barhumite
note: a Barchumite, or native of Bachurim

name: Kinah
dictNote: An elegy, a city in the extreme south of Judah (Josh. 15:22). It was probably not far from the Dead Sea, in the Wady Fikreh.

name: Erech
dictNote: (LXX., “Orech”), length, or Moon-town, one of the cities of Nimrod’s kingdom in the plain of Shinar (Gen. 10:10); the Orchoe of the Greeks and Romans. It was probably the city of the Archevites, who were transplanted to Samaria by Asnapper (Ezra 4:9). It lay on the left bank of the Euphrates, about 120 miles south-east of Babylon, and is now represented by the mounds and ruins of Warka. It appears to have been the necropolis of the Assyrian kings, as the whole region is strewed with bricks and the remains of coffins. “Standing on the summit of the principal edifice, called the Buwarizza, a tower 200 feet square in the centre of the ruins, the beholder is struck with astonishment at the enormous accumulation of mounds and ancient relics at his feet. An irregular circle, nearly 6 miles in circumference, is defined by the traces of an earthen rampart, in some places 40 feet high.”

name: Claudia
dictNote: A female Christian mentioned in 2 Tim. 4:21. It is a conjecture having some probability that she was a British maiden, the daughter of king Cogidunus, who was an ally of Rome, and assumed the name of the emperor, his patron, Tiberius Claudius, and that she was the wife of Pudens.

name: Sapphira
dictNote: Sapphira conspired with her husband Ananias to sell property and lie to the apostles about donating the full proceeds, and when Peter confronted her with the same question he'd put to her husband, unaware Ananias was already dead, she repeated the lie and immediately died the same way.

name: Hareph
dictNote: (a plucking off), a name occurring in the genealogies of Judah as a son of Caleb and as “father of Bethgader.” (1 Chronicles 2:51) only.

name: Philetus
note: amiable; Philetus, an opposer of Christianity
dictNote: Amiable, with Hymenaeus, at Ephesus, said that the “resurrection was past already” (2 Tim. 2:17, 18). This was a Gnostic heresy held by the Nicolaitanes. (See ALEXANDER [4].)

name: Bethesda
note: house of kindness; Beth-esda, a pool in Jerusalem

secondTemple.excerpt:
one well known at Rome.--Ibid.
(23) I take this Bezetha to be that small hill adjoining to the north side of the temple, whereon was the hospital with five porticoes or cloisters, and beneath which was the sheep pool of Bethesda; into which an angel or messenger, at a certain season, descended, and where he or they who were the \"first put into the pool\" were cured, John 5:1 etc.

dictNote: House of mercy, a reservoir (Gr. kolumbethra, “a swimming bath”) with five porches, close to the sheep-gate or market (Neh. 3:1; John 5:2). Eusebius the historian (A.D. 330) calls it “the sheep-pool.” It is also called “Bethsaida” and “Beth-zatha” (John 5:2, R.V. marg.). Under these “porches” or colonnades were usually a large number of infirm people waiting for the “troubling of the water.” It is usually identified with the modern so-called Fountain of the Virgin, in the valley of the Kidron, and not far from the Pool of Siloam (q.v.); and also with the Birket Israel, a pool near the mouth of the valley which runs into the Kidron south of “St. Stephen’s Gate.” Others again identify it with the twin pools called the “Souterrains,” under the convent of the Sisters of Zion, situated in what must have been the rock-hewn ditch between Bezetha and the fortress of Antonia. But quite recently Schick has discovered a large tank, as sketched here, situated about 100 feet north-west of St. Anne’s Church, which is, as he contends, very probably the Pool of Bethesda. No certainty as to its identification, however, has as yet been arrived at. (See FOUNTAIN; GIHON.)

name: Eglaim
dictNote: Two ponds, (Isa. 15:8), probably En-eglaim of Ezek. 47:10.

name: Azbuk
dictNote: (strong devastation), father or ancestor of Nehemiah, the prince of part of Bethzur. (Nehemiah 3:16)

name: Ziphion

name: Anna
dictNote: Grace, an aged widow, the daughter of Phanuel. She was a “prophetess,” like Miriam, Deborah, and Huldah (2 Chr. 34:22). After seven years of married life her husband died, and during her long widowhood she daily attended the temple services. When she was eighty-four years old, she entered the temple at the moment when the aged Simeon uttered his memorable words of praise and thanks to God that he had fulfilled his ancient promise in sending his Son into the world (Luke 2:36, 37).

dictNote: A city (now Tripoli) in Upper Libya, North Africa, founded by a colony of Greeks (B.C. 630). It contained latterly a large number of Jews, who were introduced into the city by Ptolemy, the son of Lagus, because he thought they would contribute to the security of the place. They increased in number and influence; and we are thus prepared for the frequent references to them in connection with the early history of Christianity. Simon, who bore our Lord’s cross, was a native of this place (Matt. 27:32; Mark 15:21). Jews from Cyrene were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10); and Cyrenian Jews had a synagogue at Jerusalem (6:9). Converts belonging to Cyrene contributed to the formation of the first Gentile church at Antioch (11:20). Among “the prophets and teachers” who “ministered to the Lord at Antioch” was Lucius of Cyrene (13:1).

secondTemple.excerpt: And he set over them taskmasters to afflict them with slavery; and they built strong 2 cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses, and they built all the walls and all the fortifications which had fallen in the cities of Egypt.

dictNote: Egyptian, Pa-Tum, “house of Tum,” the sun-god, one of the “treasure” cities built for Pharaoh Rameses II. by the Israelites (Ex. 1:11). It was probably the Patumos of the Greek historian Herodotus. It has now been satisfactorily identified with Tell-el-Maskhuta, about 12 miles west of Ismailia, and 20 east of Tel-el-Kebir, on the southern bank of the present Suez Canal. Here have recently (1883) been discovered the ruins of supposed grain-chambers, and other evidences to show that this was a great “store city.” Its immense ruin-heaps show that it was built of bricks, and partly also of bricks without straw. Succoth (Ex. 12:37) is supposed by some to be the secular name of this city, Pithom being its sacred name. This was the first halting-place of the Israelites in their exodus. It has been argued (Dr. Lansing) that these “store” cities “were residence cities, royal dwellings, such as the Pharaohs of old, the Kings of Israel, and our modern Khedives have ever loved to build, thus giving employment to the superabundant muscle of their enslaved peoples, and making a name for themselves.”

Some have supposed that the Russians are here meant, as one of the three Scythian tribes of whom Magog was the prince. They invaded the land of Judah in the days of Josiah. Herodotus, the Greek historian, says: “For twenty-eight years the Scythians ruled over Asia, and things were turned upside down by their violence and contempt.” (See BETHSHEAN.)

name: Asrielites
note: an Asrielite (collectively) or descendant of Asriel

name: Shunites
note: a Shunite (collectively) or descendants of Shuni

name: En-mishpat
dictNote: (fount of judgment). (Genesis 14:7) [Kadesh, Kadeshbarnea]

name: Ummah
dictNote: Vicinity, a town of Asher (Josh. 19:30).

name: Adoraim
dictNote: (double mound), a fortified city built by Rehoboam, (2 Chronicles 11:9) in Judah. Adoraim is probably the same place with Adora, 1Ma 13:20 Unless that be Dor, on the seacoast below Carmel. Robinson identifies it with Dura, a “large village” on a rising ground west of Hebron.

name: Zaanan
dictNote: Place of flocks, mentioned only in Micah 1:11. It may be identified with Zenan, in the plain country of Judah (Josh. 15:37).

name: Hannathon
dictNote: (gracious), one of the cities of Zebulun. (Joshua 19:14)

name: Hadlai
dictNote: Resting, an Ephraimite; the father of Amasa, mentioned in 2 Chr. 28:12.

name: Persis
note: a Persian woman; Persis, a Christian female
dictNote: A female Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes (Rom. 16:12). She is spoken of as “beloved,” and as having “laboured much in the Lord.”

name: Armageddon
dictNote: Occurs only in Rev. 16:16 (R.V., “Har-Magedon”), as symbolically designating the place where the “battle of that great day of God Almighty” (ver. 14) shall be fought. The word properly means the “mount of Megiddo.” It is the scene of the final conflict between Christ and Antichrist. The idea of such a scene was suggested by the Old Testament great battle-field, the plain of Esdraelon (q.v.).

name: Abel-mizraim
dictNote: Meadow of Egypt, or mourning of Egypt, a place “beyond,” i.e., on the west of Jordan, at the “threshing-floor of Atad.” Here the Egyptians mourned seventy days for Jacob (Gen. 50:4-11). Its site is unknown.

name: Abdeel

secondTemple.excerpt: Of this wife were born to Ishmael twelve sons: Nabaioth, Kedar, Abdeel, Mabsam, Idumas, Masmaos, Massaos, Chodad, Theman, Jetur, Naphesus, Kadmas.

dictNote: Servant of God, (Jer. 36:26), the father of Shelemiah.

name: Beth-lebaoth
dictNote: (house of lionesses), a town in the lot of Simeon, (Joshua 19:6) in the extreme south of Judah. [ (Joshua 15:32) Lebaoth] In (1 Chronicles 4:31) the name is given BETH-BIREI.

name: Bealiah
dictNote: Whose Lord is Jehovah, a Benjamite, one of David’s thirty heroes of the sling and bow (1 Chr. 12:5).

name: Tibhath
dictNote: (extension), a city of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, (1 Chronicles 18:8) which in 2Sam 8:8 Is called Betah. Its exact Position is unknown.

name: Nehushta

secondTemple.excerpt: And this was the end of King Jehoiakim, when he had lived thirty six years, and of them reigned eleven.12 But Jehoiachin succeeded him in the Kingdom: whose mothers name was Nehushta: she was a citizen of Jerusalem.

dictNote: Copper, the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem, and the wife of Jehoiakin (2 Kings 24:8), king of Judah.

name: Eutychus
note: well- fated, i.e. fortunate; Eutychus, a young man

secondTemple.excerpt: Agrippa praying [to God] (for they two sat by themselves), that “Tiberius might soon go off the stage, and leave the government to Caius, who was in every respect more worthy of it.” Now Eutychus, who was Agrippa’s freed man, and drove his chariot, heard these words: and at that time said nothing of them.

When they were in these circumstances, Cherea was not able to contain the anger he had, and promised, that if they desired an emperor, he would give them one, if any one would bring him the watchword from Eutychus.

dictNote: Fortunate, (Acts 20:9-12), a young man of Troas who fell through drowsiness from the open window of the third floor of the house where Paul was preaching, and was “taken up dead.” The lattice-work of the window being open to admit the air, the lad fell out and down to the court below. Paul restored him to life again. (Comp. 1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34.)

name: Adadah
dictNote: (festival or boundary), one of the cities in the extreme south of Judah, named with Dimonah and Kedesh. (Joshua 15:22)

name: Ahasai
dictNote: (whom Jehovah holds), a priest, ancestor of Maasiai, (Nehemiah 11:13) called Jahzerah in (1 Chronicles 9:12)

name: Beri
dictNote: (a well), son of Zophah, of the tribe of Asher. (1 Chronicles 7:36)

name: Rephael
dictNote: Healed of God, one of Shemaiah’s sons. He and his brethren, on account of their “strength for service,” formed one of the divisions of the temple porters (1 Chr. 26:7, 8).

name: Beth-haccerem
dictNote: House of a vineyard, a place in the tribe of Judah (Neh. 3:14) where the Benjamites were to set up a beacon when they heard the trumpet against the invading army of the Babylonians (Jer. 6:1). It is probable that this place is the modern ‘Ain Karim, or “well of the vineyards,” near which there is a ridge on which are cairns which may have served as beacons of old, one of which is 40 feet high and 130 in diameter.

name: Helkath-hazzurim
note: Chelkath Hats-tsurim, a place in Palestine
dictNote: Plot of the sharp blades, or the field of heroes, (2 Sam. 2:16). After the battle of Gilboa, so fatal to Saul and his house, David, as divinely directed, took up his residence in Hebron, and was there anointed king over Judah. Among the fugitives from Gilboa was Ish-bosheth, the only surviving son of Saul, whom Abner, Saul’s uncle, took across the Jordan to Mahanaim, and there had him proclaimed king. Abner gathered all the forces at his command and marched to Gibeon, with the object of wresting Judah from David. Joab had the command of David’s army of trained men, who encamped on the south of the pool, which was on the east of the hill on which the town of Gibeon was built, while Abner’s army lay on the north of the pool. Abner proposed that the conflict should be decided by twelve young men engaging in personal combat on either side. So fiercely did they encounter each other that “they caught every man his fellow by the head, and thrust his sword in his fellow’s side; so they fell down together: wherefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim.” The combat of the champions was thus indecisive, and there followed a severe general engagement between the two armies, ending in the total rout of the Israelites under Abner. The general result of this battle was that “David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker” (2 Sam. 3:1). (See GIBEON.)

name: Apelles
